column4: ch-005 chunk 1 (Inikori, volume of the trade)
column5: Inikori (GHA V, 1992) dates export slave trade from black Africa to the Mediterranean, Middle East and Asia from about the ninth century (small annual numbers) and the transatlantic trade from the 16th century; he argues the trade was key to a core-periphery 'Atlantic economic order' (a dependency-school thesis, his framework). On numbers he says post-1976 studies (his own, Palmer, Vila Vilar, Rout, Eltis, Stein) find Curtin's 1969 figures much too low, especially for the 16th-17th centuries, and infers a 40 per cent upward revision of Curtin's about 11 million to about 15.4 million; he criticises Lovejoy's 1982 'new estimate' as mixing revised and unrevised figures. Compare with Voyages' about 12.5 million embarked: this chapter predates Voyages (1999 onward) and its 15.4 million is an inference, not a count [CONTESTED].

Inikori gives Trans-Saharan and Red Sea/Indian Ocean exports as about 6.86 million for 1500-1890 (Austen 3,956,000 plus 2,900,000; preferred to Mauny's 10 million for 1400-1900), so about 22 million exported from black Africa 1500-1890 by his sum; the rest of the chunk is his argument that Atlantic trade and slavery drove Europe's capitalist transformation (European bullion, plantation sugar, trade growth figures). That is a dependency-school thesis, not a settled result [CONTESTED]. Chunks 3 to 5 of this chapter are unread.

Inikori's argument continues with the Americas: slave plantations in the US South (697,000 slaves in 1790, 3,117,000 in 1850 = 34.7%), Brazil (African-origin people 61.2% of the population in 1798), the Caribbean (Barbados, Jamaica, Leewards: 22,500 slaves in 1660, 130,000 in 1713) and contraband imports to Spanish America (Cartagena registered figures far below real ones, Vila Vilar). He claims US industrialisation up to 1860 rested on southern slave plantations; this is the chapter's thesis [CONTESTED]. Figures are from cited secondary tables (Potter, Dunn, Sheridan) and are reported by him; use for the Atlantic side of Module 8 only with the dependency framing stated.

Inikori argues black Africa's population 'declined absolutely from at least 1650 to 1850': exports of about 22 million 1500-1890 (15.4 million Atlantic, 6.9 million Sahara, Red Sea and Indian Ocean), females 32.9% of a 404,705-slave sample (Bight of Benin about 50% female, Angola about 32%), plus deaths in wars and on the march; regions most depopulated: Bights of Benin and Biafra and Congo-Angola. He cites Wrigley, Shaw and Posnansky for population growth before 1500 (West Africa about 3 million in 1000 CE to about 20 million in 1500 on Shaw's calculation) and says African economies were 'undeveloped' in 1500 and the trade 'laid the foundation for dependency'. Compare with Manning (almost no growth 1750-1850, via Reader), Rodney, and Eltis; 'absolute decline' is stronger than Manning's model and is a position [CONTESTED]. Dutch Gold Coast officers (Abramsz 1679) report war after guns arrived.

Inikori says the export trade stimulated wars and military aristocracies (Dutch officers 1679 and 1730 and Equiano quoted as witnesses), turned dependence into chattel slavery, kept states small and unstable, and that legitimate commerce later extended slave production; he concludes that the Atlantic order and England's and the north-east US industrial revolutions 'could not have occurred at the time they did' without African slave labour, and that Africa entered the 20th century backward as a result. These are strong, single-author causal claims (one side of a debate with Eltis, Manning, Thornton); the quoted contemporaries support the wars link but not the full thesis. Use as a named position in Module 8 [CONTESTED].

Alagoa (GHA V, 1992): languages of the region show long stability (Ijo separated from its neighbours over 5,000 years by glottochronology, Yoruba and Igala about 2,000), so continuity should temper claims about the Europeans' impact; Portuguese reached Benin in 1486. Dahomey: Akinjogbin's view that the slave trade and Oyo shaped it (Abomey founded about 1625 by migrants from Allada, 'perforated pot' idea of an absolute state, Agaja's conquests 1724-27, tribute to Oyo after 1730, depression from about 1767, Gezo's dynasty 1818); Peukert's revision says the Dahomean state made no more than 20 per cent of foreign trade, the Atlantic trade only about 2.5 per cent of the economy, and slaves and guns were not the main items (Brazilian tobacco outweighed guns): a challenge to the slave-trade-driven story [CONTESTED]. Yoruba: Ife founder Oduduwa tradition read as migration about 1,000 years ago into already settled land; Ife art dated about 900-1300 CE against Nok (to 200 CE); 'Mecca' in tradition read as a place across the Niger, not the Middle East; Oyo power came from cavalry and archers, officials of slave origin, Sango cult, driven from Old Oyo in the 15th century and recovering by 1500; Oyo stopped by forest (Ijesha), and stayed out of direct European trade and guns before the 19th century. Module 5.

column4: ch-016 chunk 2 (Niger Delta, Igboland, Cross River)
column5: Alagoa: Eastern Delta city-states (Bonny, Kalabari, Okrika, Nembe) took up kingship from about the 13th century and the slave trade accelerated their change; Igboland farmed yams at least 3,000 years ago, Nri divine kingship and Igbo-Ukwu bronzes from a different tradition from Ife and Benin, Aro traders used the Arochukwu oracle and mercenaries and developed from about the 17th century; Efik at Calabar and the Ekpe society; Itsekiri as middlemen; cassava reached the Delta by the 17th century and parts of Igboland two to three centuries later. His conclusion sorts communities into three: middlemen (Delta states, Calabar), active procurers (Dahomey, Aro) and victims (parts of Yorubaland, Igboland, Ibibioland), and says whether the slave trade brought isolated regions out of isolation is 'speculative'; the slave-trade era is remembered as 'a bad dream'. Module 5 and 8.

Vansina (1992): over half a million contemporary pages on the region 1500-1800 survive; Kongo's founding date is unknown (some place the process from the ninth century, others no later than about 1400 and at least a century earlier; this corrects the vol. IV chapter's 'thirteenth-fourteenth century' with a range); Nimi Lukeni founded Mbanza Kongo by alliance with the Kabunga and the Mbata king and by conquest; population of the kingdom proper 'two million' most accepted (others half a million to eight million); royalty elective with a twelve-member council including four women; kings centralised through appointed governors, nzimbu shells from Luanda island, a royal guard of slaves 16,000-20,000 in the late 16th century; Afonso I (reigned 1506-43, Christian since 1491) made Catholicism the state religion, his son Henrique was bishop 1518-36, the slave trade grew from 1514, he tried to control it and in 1526 to abolish it and failed; civil war after 1665 destroyed the old kingdom. The word for slave also meant war captive. Module 6.

Vansina: Afonso's attempt to stop the trade in 1526 failed; slave exports from Kongo about 4,000-5,000 a year to 1540, then 6,000-7,000; kings guarded copper and iron from Portuguese prospecting; imports of cloth and wine absorbed the revenue by Afonso's end; 1561 Kongo cut itself off from Portugal; the 'Jaga' invasion about 1567-71 is of unestablished identity (a name for barbarian warriors; drought explanation has no evidence) and Portugal reconquered 1571-75; Angola founded 1575, Luanda 1576, Ndongo war to 1671, Queen Nzinga (regent 1624, queen 1626) in Matamba, Imbangala state of Kasanje in the 1630s; Luanda exported 10,000-13,000 slaves a year early on (11,000 legal in 1625); Dutch took Luanda 1641-48; nzimbu lost two-thirds of its value by 1619 as Portugal imported other shells; maize arrived between 1548 and 1583 and manioc soon after 1600, improving yields; smallpox by 1560; Mbwila 1665 ended the old kingdom (Antonio I killed). Module 6 and 8.

column4: ch-020 chunk 3 (after Mbwila; social change; religion)
column5: After Mbwila (1665) civil war destroyed Mbanza Kongo in 1666, it was abandoned 1678 and re-entered only in 1709; Kimpa Vita (Dona Beatriz) preached Antonianism from 1704 and was burnt as a heretic in 1706; economy: Brazilian capital ran the Angola trade (Luanda exports 10,000+ a year), English, French and Dutch competed on the Loango coast, the Vili caravans bought rather than raided; Kasanje grew on the Kwango as slave routes shifted. Kongo's three strata (nobles, rustics, slaves) compressed to two; the matrilineal clan (mvila) is attested only in the 19th century (Vansina warns against reading 19th-century institutions back); Christianity mixed with the old nkisi ideas (Capuchins from 1645 baptised many), Garcia II nicknamed 'the sorcerer'; claim that this religion was the source of Haitian vodou is Vansina's statement without proof here [THIN EVIDENCE]. Module 6 and 8.

column4: ch-020 chunk 4 (Kongo art; 18th-century Loango coast trade)
column5: Vansina: Kongo kept its Catholicism after 1700 (the claim that it lost it is false; missionaries failed to recognise it); art shows continuity and assimilation, Christian influence on Kongo statuary is 'baseless' as a general claim; Gabon white masks and Kuba raffia velvet may derive from Kongo styles. 18th century: networks, not states, organised the region; about one million slaves put aboard on the Loango coast 1660-1797 (Curtin, Lovejoy), perhaps two million people taken counting deaths on the routes (his note says doubling is not an exaggeration), a third women; 50,000 guns a year imported in the second half of the century (Martin, 'rather high' beside Van Alstein, tens of thousands); demand rose from 1665 to 1755 and peaked 1755-97; Vili and Bobangi caravans and river carriers; brokers (mercadores) and the 'parcel' of goods against the 'standard slave' adult male; areas specialised and lost crafts (Tio gave up iron-smelting and boat-building); Loango's royal line extinct about 1750 and no king from 1787 for almost two centuries; Tio civil war from about 1780 with the nkobi ideology. Population effects 'largely unknown' but fell in old Kongo and Mayombe. Module 6 and 8.

Vansina on Angola: the trade was fragmented (Portuguese exporters, Brazilian brokers, shippers, Luanda and Benguela dealers, Afro-Portuguese caravaneers, African lords) and each link tried to shift 'the slave risk' down the chain; an estimate quoted by Miller that half the slaves bought died before the port and 40 per cent more at Luanda is called exaggerated by Vansina (the author was a rival company's servant) though 'credible'; losses at sea 10 to 15 per cent (Lovejoy); parcel (hanzo) supplied on credit to caravaneers; Lunda empire grew in the 18th century with Kazembe founded after 1750; Yaka state on the Kwango between 1740 and 1760; Angolan revenue about 1800 was 88 per cent from slaves for Brazil and under 5 per cent from ivory; Lozi reached by caravans before 1794; footnote: the 1,032,000 Loango-coast embarked figure doubles to about 2 million people and 'might be nearer 3 million' (his judgement), and he disputes Thornton's low estimate of women and children shipped. Module 6 and 8.

column4: ch-012 chunk 1 (Abitbol, end of Songhay and the Pashalik)
column5: Abitbol (GHA V Ch 11): al-Mansur's motives were gold, slaves for Moroccan sugar, Taghaza salt and jihad; Songhai had developed new salt deposits at Taghaza al-Ghizlan (Taoudeni) and lost Taghaza in 1585; Moroccan column of three to four thousand soldiers left Marrakesh 30 October 1590 under Judar Pasha, reached the Niger 1 March 1591, defeated Askiya Ishaq II at Tondibi on 12 March 1591 with guns; causes: struggles since Askiya Muhammad's fall in 1529, Balama al-Sadduq's rebellion at Timbuktu, Portuguese coastal trade, military reverses in Dendi, Borgu and Mossi (slave sources), epidemics and drought, and no unifying ethnic frame, with the empire's centre of gravity in conquered Timbuktu and Jenne; Mahmud b. Zarqun destroyed Songhai power 1592-4 and sent scholars including Ahmad Baba into exile; Zarqun killed 1594; Moroccans held only river garrisons (kasabas at Jenne, Timbuktu, Gao etc.), did not change local administration; Morocco stopped appointing officials from 1618 leaving the Arma; 145 pashas appointed at Timbuktu 1646-1825, rotating among three divisions; Tuareg Kel-Tadmekket beat the Arma 1737; Bambara of Segu never entered Jenne; Kunta entered Timbuktu on the eve of the Fulbe conquest 1825-6. Module 4 [PROBABLE]; chronicle sources named.

column4: ch-012 chunk 2 (Abitbol, Dendi, Segu, Tuareg, famines)
column5: Abitbol (GHA V Ch 11): Askiya Nuh held Dendi by ambush, was deposed 1599 and the Dendi Songhai broke into small kingdoms, treaty with Morocco 1630; after the Mansa of Mali's defeat at Jenne in 1599 Bambara kafu rebelled against Marka chiefs in the mid-17th century, Biton Kulibali (c.1710-c.1755) founded Segu, Ngolo Diarra after 1766, Monzon (1789-1808); Masa-si Kaarta; Kong Joola attack on Segu about 1739-45; Fulbe preponderant in Macina; Tuareg beat the Arma at Toya in May 1737 killing 300-350 including the pasha, siege of Timbuktu 1770; Kunta mediation; Jenne lived 'alone and independent' until the Fulbe of Macina conquered it 1818-19 (not a Bambara protectorate); Pashas paid allegiance to Saadian sultans until 1659 and renewed it to the Alawites, whose policy aimed at Mauritania; Abid black army; famine of 1639, seven-year shortage 1711-18, terrible famine from 1738, famine and plague 1741, plague 1748-9, 1762-6, 1786-96; nomad-farmer conflicts each hot season; Jenne supply region San; wheat only after the Moroccans. Module 4 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE for numbers killed].

column4: ch-012 chunk 3 (Abitbol, trade routes and marabouts)
column5: Abitbol (GHA V Ch 11): after 1591 the Dar'a-Taghaza-Timbuktu route became the royal road but within fifty years the network reverted to medieval routes (Sus, Tafilalet); Atlantic route revived in the 1620s under the Alawites; Juula network from Jenne to Kong, Asante and Bure; Yarse Mossi side-roads; Moroccan exports (books, silk, tobacco, sugar, firearms); salt played a small part since the Niger towns used separate azalai from Taoudeni; amount of gold exported never again equalled that after the Moroccan conquest; slave exports rose after Mawlay Isma'il formed the Abid army; gum arabic and Mogador port in the 18th century; the period was not cultural stagnation: all inhabitants of Timbuktu and Jenne could read Arabic (Caillie), the Timbuktu ta'rikhs were all written between the 17th and 19th centuries; marabout groups (zawaya) emerged in the second half of the 17th century from Senegal to Air and their Qadiriyya networks (Kunta) fed the 18th-19th-century jihads (Abd al-Qadir, Usman dan Fodio's teacher Jibril, Hamdallahi, Umar Tall). Module 4 [PROBABLE]; note the chronicles' dating.

Laya (GHA V Ch 16): sources uneven, Kano Chronicle has errors of translation, new editions urgently needed; periods: 1500-1620 (Kano and Katsina conflict, Kebbi dominant in the west), 1620-1730 (Kano toward a caliphate, Zamfara and Gobir consolidating, Kwararafa attacks), 1730-1808 (Zamfara collapse, Gobir at its peak); Askiya Muhammad's Azbin campaign led to Kebbi's independence in 1516 under Kanta, Songhai failed against Kebbi about 1533 and made peace 1553; Borno army of 100 000 (his figure) beaten by Kebbi 1561; Kano-Katsina wars (11-year war under Rumfa c.1463-99, Kutumbi killed c.1648, peace c.1649-51 inspired by fear of Kwararafa); Kano population took refuge at Daura 1582-1618, 1653, 1671; Kwararafa defeated by Borno 1680; Gwanja-Kano-Borno route opened 1438-52 by Abdullahi Burja; Agades replaced Takedda as caravan centre in the 15th century, making Katsina a terminus; Laya doubts that the Kano-Katsina wars were simply a struggle for the trans-Saharan terminus; the Kano chronology (Palmer) is approximate. Module 4 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE on dates and numbers].

column4: ch-017 chunk 2 (Laya, Kebbi, Gobir, Zamfara and Hausa government)
column5: Laya (GHA V Ch 16): Kebbi under the Kanta rose after 1561 as the strongest Hausa military power but there is no proof of tribute from other states or of conquering Songhai; Gobir moved from Azbin to Birnin Lalle about 1450, driven out by Tuareg about 1600, to Gwaran Rama about 1685-90 and later Alkalawa; Zamfara strong in the mid-17th century under Muslim sovereigns, beat Kebbi's 6000-man army 1674, defeated Kano at Yargana under Sharif (1703-31); Kebbi eliminated about 1722; Gobir under Soba and Babari beat Kano at Dumi and destroyed Birnin Zamfara about 1762; Damagaram sultanate founded early 18th century; Hausa government: Sarki chosen by an electoral college (the Nine in Zamfara, Gobir and Kano; four in Katsina), titles like Galadima, Madawaki, Ajiya, a powerful royal sister or queen mother (Madaki Auwa, Kano), guild representatives, autochthonous groups and immigrants (Fulbe, Tuareg) with their own officials, city governors semi-independent; Laya says the Kebbi chronology is doubtful and Maikassoua's dates for Gobir are pre-publication. Module 4 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-017 chunk 3 (Laya, Hausa military, taxes, aristocracy, farming)
column5: Laya (GHA V Ch 16): Kebbi's rise brought military leaders to the fore (Kunduda in Kebbi, Kaura in Katsina, Ubandawaki in Zamfara and Gobir); horses came from Azbin and Borno, heavy cavalry with quilted armour (lifidi), Kebbi had a river flotilla; firearms: introduced to Kano by a Borno prince in 1421-38 (a puzzling claim), imported from Nupe in 1731-43, Babba Zaki (1768-76) first fusiliers bodyguard; Songhai Dendi massacred 400 Moroccan fusiliers but threw their rifles into rivers; Hausa states deliberately neglected rifles (despite wealth); taxes: kudin kasa (land tax, Kano one-eighth under Naguji c.1197-1247), kudin sana'a, kudin hito (customs), jangali (livestock tax first levied by Kutumbi c.1623-48 as 280 cattle), kudin haki; gifts (gaisuwa); spoils of raids (Kano took 400 horses and 60 sets of trappings; Kutumbi left 500 slaves at Indabo); Sharif (c.1703-31) seven oppressive taxes; Kumbari (1731-43) loved his advisers and hated the people; royal slaves and eunuchs as officials; aristocracy grew rich through pillage; Diagne 'oligarchical monarchy' versus Usman's 'urban centres' model; agriculture: manoma farmers, gayya mutual aid, fertiliser, rotation, Feast of Thousands (bukin duku), Sarkin Noma; Fulbe and Tuareg grazing, cattle burial site in the Sahara dated 1435. Module 4 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE on firearms dates].

column4: ch-017 chunk 4 (Laya, crafts, trade, social relations and slavery)
column5: Laya (GHA V Ch 16): Hausa crafts (iron, leather, weaving, dyeing) were highly specialised with guilds; external trade in Hausa hands with Wangara, Juula, Mossi and Kanuri; markets at Agades, Bilma, Katsina, Kano, Zaria, Birnin Gwari, Yawuri; flows: Azbin sent horses, salt, swords, Hausaland sent slaves, cloth, millet, hides, iron, gold dust and kola from Gwanja, Borno sent horses and natron; Hausa farmers, tributaries and slaves all members of the political community; attajirai merchants and scholars linked; Arabs left Kano for Katsina over Kumbari's taxes; slavery: Kano Chronicle says Galadima Dawuda took 21 000 slaves in a campaign in 1438-52 settled in 21 Indabo villages (Laya calls it a genuine slaving expedition, not population movement, against Hiskett), Mai Arku of Kanem (1023-67) had 900 slaves in three places, Kwararafa sent slaves to Kano rulers, royal slave estates (Tsagero, Gozaki cotton estates), bawa to bacucane house-born slave transition; the lot of slaves 'not preferable to that of the talaka'; the political divide became wealth (attajirai) versus talakawa. Module 4/8 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE on 21 000 and 900].

column4: ch-017 chunk 5 (Laya, Islam and scholars, conclusion)
column5: Laya (GHA V Ch 16): Islamisation at the start of the 16th century was confined to traders and the political elite; scholars arrived in Kano under Kisoki (1509-65) many from Borno, Katsina scholars from the west (Mali), Zamfara first Muslim sovereign about 1670; scholars negotiated the Kano-Katsina peace 1648-51; ajami script used in Kano and Katsina in the 16th century; Katsina scholars al-Maghili's successor lines, Dan Marina c.1650, Muhammad al-Kashinawi d. c.1741, al-Barnawi d. c.1755; Jibril dan Umaru of Adar, teacher of Usman and Abdullahi dan Fodio, who regarded himself as his disciple and successor; before the jihad tension between rulers and scholars; Laya's conclusion: neither wheel nor windmill nor rifle used, but production and processing advanced; no Hausa state disappeared 1500-1800; cowrie introduced into Kano under Sharif; natural calamities 1539-64, 1639-88, 1697-1715, 1729-50. (The file's end runs into Barkindo's Chapter 17 on Kanem-Borno: Safuwa moved to Borno 1382-87, Ali Gaji c.1465-97 built Birnin Gazargamu about 1472, claimed caliphal investiture about 1484; to be logged with ch-018.) Module 4 [PROBABLE].

Barkindo (GHA V Ch 17): Safuwa moved to Borno 1382-87, Ali Gaji (c.1465-97) built Birnin Gazargamu about 1472, claimed caliphal investiture about 1484 (before Askiya Muhammad in 1496-8); Borno-Kebbi war about 1561 over Agades which Borno appears to have lost; Songhai expeditions against Agades 1501 and 1515, Borno took it about 1532; Idris Alawoma (1564-96) reached the apogee: Turkish gunmen, larger boats, pacified a metropolitan province of about 20 000 sq km, expelled unmalleable groups (Ngafata, Talata, Dugurti), settled Kanem groups (Tubu, Koyam, Kulu, Shuwa Arabs), ravaged three Kanem valleys, Kanem state partitioned with the Bulala by the 1580s; regional economy: fishing and natron, Gazargamu as nerve centre; exports of slaves, eunuchs, skins, ivory, perfumes, gold across the Sahara, imports horses, armour, copper; Alawoma's diplomacy with the Ottomans (embassy about 1574, Sultan Murad III reply 5 May 1577, tribute of Fezzan raised from 1140 to 3000 mithqal about 1571, arms not the main aim) and with Morocco (about 1583, bay'a to al-Mansur disputed); Barkindo cautions that sources are one-sided. Module 4 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-018 chunk 2 (Barkindo, Kanuri, Borno government, golden age)
column5: Barkindo (GHA V Ch 17): Alawoma died in a campaign against Bagirmi (assassinated by a Gamergu), his death did not collapse Borno; the Kanuri emerged as an ethnic group by the early 17th century from Magumi and Chadic-speaking peoples; Kanuri society stratified (Kontuowa nobility, tala'a commoners), fired-brick walls mid-16th to early 18th century; scholars of two kinds (office-holding court ulama and austere rural malamti); mai as Amir al-Mu'minin, secluded sacred king, selected from maina princes, from c.1677 rival candidates eliminated (learned from the Ottomans); majlis of twelve, chidi fiefs; income zakat, tolls, tribute, booty; Barkindo says the 17th century, not the 16th, was Borno's golden age (Umar b. Idris c.1619-39 set up Galadima at Nguru and Alifa of Mao; Ali b. Umar c.1639-77 Borno dominant, controlling salt at Muniyo, Bilma and around Lake Chad, 'fourth sultanate of the Islamic world'); Tripoli's Muhammad Sakizli proposed a monopoly c.1636; maize, tomatoes and pawpaw came via Egypt (Kanuri names mean Egyptian); late-18th-century crisis under Ali b. Dunama (c.1742-92): Tuareg took Bilma salt about 1759, Bagirmi and Wadai broke away, Mandara revolted c.1781, Gobir 1785, famines drove Fulbe into Hausaland, so the jihad context. Module 4 [PROBABLE]; this corrects the idea that Borno peaked in the 16th century.

column4: ch-018 chunk 3 (Barkindo, jihad and the mai)
column5: Barkindo (GHA V Ch 17): when the jihad broke out the Hausa client-rulers called on the mai as caliph and patron, who could not help or even prevent his own expulsion from the capital, showing the caliph's primacy had been lost; yet the Safuwa system in metropolitan Borno survived with modification into the 20th century. Module 4 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-014 chunk 1 (Wondji, Upper Guinean coast sources and peoples)
column5: Wondji (GHA V Ch 13): Upper Guinea coast has over 100 ethnic groups, sources unevenly Portuguese and plentiful only for Senegambia, Rivers Coast and Gold Coast to Niger delta, archaeology in its infancy, oral tradition rarely before the 17th century, historical linguistics still at planning stage; Mande movements: peasant settlement from the 12th-13th century, Fati and Sane clans in Kaabu, then 'conquering migration of Tiramaghan Traore, one of Sundiata's retired generals' which Wondji dates at the end of the 15th century (this conflicts with Person in vol IV who places Tiramaghan in the 13th century, an internal inconsistency in the series); causes: collateral succession pushed princes west, traders and farmers also moved; Casamance Bainuk, Joola, Balante before the 15th century, Fulbe from Macina in the 15th; Yengema excavation (Sierra Leone) suggests occupation since the 3rd millennium BC; Temne reached the sea only at end of 16th century; Kru early on the coast (sickle-cell evidence); Vai migrated 1500-1550 for salt and trade; Mane-Sumba reached Cape Mount in 1545; mande merchants and warriors spread to the forest fringes with kola traders. Module 5 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE]; chronology conflict with vol IV flagged [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-014 chunk 2 (Wondji, Mane invasion and 17th-18th century movements)
column5: Wondji (GHA V Ch 13): Mane-Sumba reached Cape Mount in 1545 and were absorbed by the early 17th century; Fage thinks Mane were Mande warriors with Kru and West Atlantic auxiliaries (Sumba), Person thinks a Northern Mande aristocracy led Southern Mande warriors including the Toma; the Sapes 'kingdom' was destroyed and four kingdoms (Bullom, Loko, Bure, Sherbro) formed; 17th-18th century migrations were multidirectional, driven by the slave trade (d'Azevedo); Fulbe jihad in Futa Jallon from 1720-30 drove Tyapi, Baga and Landuma to the coast (battle of Talansam 1725-30), Soso under Soumba Toumane invaded the Baga from 1760; Mende formed in the late 1600s-early 1700s from Mande and Kisi/Bullom/Loko/Temne; Quoja and Karou hegemony from the 1620s; Kru east-west movement; sea routes: Mali linked the coast from Senegambia to the Gold Coast before the Portuguese, Joola corporations from 1312, Portuguese at Arguin 1443, Senegal and Gambia 1445-56, Sierra Leone and Liberia 1460-2, Ivory Coast 1469-70, Gold Coast 1470-1; carved ivories (Bullom/Sherbro) are the earliest African sculptures in Europe. Module 5/8 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Mane].

column4: ch-014 chunk 3 (Wondji, Kaabu, Atlantic trade companies, Karou)
column5: Wondji (GHA V Ch 13): Portuguese held supremacy to about 1560 in Upper Guinea trading by river without territorial occupation, separating Bambuk and Bure gold from the Niger and Sahara toward the Atlantic; Dutch took the monopoly (Goree 1621, El Mina 1637, Arguin 1638), 200 Dutch voyages 1593-1607, West India Company 1621, English Royal African Company 1672, French companies 1664/1685, Treaty of Utrecht 1713 asiento; no forts between Senegambia and the Gold Coast; West Atlantic societies (Joola, Temne) village societies without slaves or castes with age groups, paddy rice debate (Pelissier, Davidson), 'Kingdom of the Sapes' as confederation (Niane) or Mande-led state (Suret-Canale) undecided, and Wondji cautions against diffusionist explanations of patrilineal succession and states; Kaabu: farin of Kaabu became independent of Mali in 1537, twelve confederated Mande provinces, mansa at Kansala, Mansa Biram selling 600 slaves a year at the end of the 17th century (Cissoko); Futa Jallon jihad c.1725-30; Karou hegemony in Sierra Leone-Liberia a commercial sphere run by middlemen; Atlantic trade split the Sudanic ruling class into a military aristocracy (Bambara states) and marabout-merchants (Fulbe revolutions), Kong empire (Juula) in the 18th century. Module 5/8 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Sapes].

column4: ch-014 chunk 4 (Wondji, lancados, Afro-Portuguese, Grain Coast)
column5: Wondji (GHA V Ch 13): lancados (Portuguese 'thrown among the blacks', with Greeks, Spaniards, Indians) and their Afro-Portuguese descendants (filhos da terra) ran local trade in Upper Guinea in the 17th-18th centuries as a comprador class; Bibiana Vaz of Cacheu led the 1684-5 petition against the Cacheu Company monopoly; Jose Lopez de Moura (grandson of a Mane king) was kingmaker in Sierra Leone and destroyed the Royal African Company factory; Anglo-Africans (Tucker, Rogers, Corker, Cleveland families) numbered nearly 12 000 by 1800; Kru coast did not develop merchant groups because malaguetta crisis and poor links; the whole coast was integrated into the world market 1500-1800. Module 5/8 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-015 chunk 1 (Boahen, Lower Guinea migrations and economy)
column5: Boahen (GHA V Ch 14): 1500-1800 completed Akan, Ga-Adangbe and Ewe migrations: Akan mostly in Adansi-Amanse cradle in 1500 then dispersal in the 16th-17th centuries, large movement 1680-1730 from Kumasi, Anwianwia and Denkyira into Nzima, Aowin, Sehwi, Anyi and Baule, flow dry by the 1750s; Ewe left Notsie in the late 1500s-early 1600s fleeing king Agokoli; Ayawaso Ga settlement founded late 16th century; the Lagunaires and Anyi/Baule arose from Akan mixing with earlier peoples (Eastern and Western Akan not mutually intelligible); eight Akan matrilineal clans, each family with an abusuapanin; economy: kola, new American crops (maize, cassava, groundnuts) from the 16th-17th centuries, gold panning old and deep mining introduced by Mande in the 13th or 14th century, gold peaking in the late 1600s at about 2 000 000 oz (Garrard figure), gold mining an Akan monopoly resisting Dutch; Juula posts (Begho, Kong, Bonduku, Buna); Boahen says north-west trade did not decline after Songhai's fall but grew, and Asante expanded in the early 1700s (Gyaman, Banda, Bono) to tap it; trade with Hausa via Salaga; kola re-exported to Tripoli (Lucas 1780s); Portuguese off the Ghana coast in 1471, first Atlantic cargo of slaves to the West Indies 1518 and Virginia 1619; the coast was split into Ivory, Gold and Slave coasts with forty-two forts (Lawrence). Module 5/8 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE on gold ounces].

column4: ch-015 chunk 2 (Boahen, Gold Coast slave trade and states before Asante)
column5: Boahen (GHA V Ch 14): Gold Coast imported slaves for the mines in the 15th-16th centuries (2060 from Benin in April 1529, 80 from Sao Tome 1535), then from the mid-1600s exported them; by 1710 slaves exceeded gold in trade (Dutch factor De la Palma 1704); Daaku 5-6000 exported yearly by 1700 rising to 6-7000 in the 18th century and Curtin 474 000 for the 18th century with Curtin underestimated by 7.3-18.4% (Inikori); three reasons: sugar plantation demand from the 1640s, war captives and guns (Royal African Company shipped almost 66 000 firearms and 9000 barrels of powder 1673-1704; Inikori 49 130 368 pounds of powder 1750-1807), tribute in slaves from Denkyira, Akwamu and Asante vassals; western Akan kept exporting ivory and gold; value of exports 1750-1807 (England: 5.44m pounds non-slave versus 53.7m slaves); Boahen's thesis 'economic growth without economic development', destruction of local industry by cheap imports; coastal city-states broke from inland capitals by 1800; state formation: Ga kings by 1600 (Ayawaso capital until 1680), Akan small city-states, Adansi confederation from about 1550, Dutch map of 1629 shows 38 states, Denkyira broke from Adansi in the 1650s-60s and dominated the south-west by 1690, Akwamu conquered Ga in 1681 and expanded 1702-10; Aowin and Sehwi states, Oyoko states near Kumasi, Gyaman. Module 5/8 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Boahen's underdevelopment thesis][THIN EVIDENCE on totals].

column4: ch-015 chunk 3 (Boahen, Denkyira, Akwamu, Asante and the Akan states)
column5: Boahen (GHA V Ch 14): Denkyira and Akwamu empires had metropolitan and provincial areas, wing system (three wings Denkyira, five Akwamu and Asante), offices of Batahene, Sanaahene, Gyaasehene, Akyeamehene; eighteenth-century Gold Coast politics was not only Asante: Aowin sacked Kumasi in 1718-19 under Ebri Moro, Anyi states (Sanwi, Ndenye, Bettie, Moronou) and Baule (Alanguira from Denkyira about 1700, Assabu led by Queen Abla Poku after Osei Tutu's death in 1717), Nzima (Apollonia), Bron; Asante conquered Denkyira in 1699-1701, then Sehwi 1701-2, Twifo 1712-13, Wassa 1713 and 1726, Aowin 1715-21, Nzima 1715, Ndenye 1715, Wenchi 1711-14, Bono 1723-4, Bron 1731-40, Gonja 1732; Akyem Abuakwa beat Akwamu 1731; Asante conquered Akyem 1742, Ga 1744-5, Dagomba 1744; Asante structure: metropolitan Asante within 50 km of Kumasi, five wings, Golden Stool, Asanteman Council, adamfo client-state system with commissioners from 1760-1800; why: gold and kola middlemen, motive to reach the coast, free from European interference, guns and wing formation, strong leaders (Osei Tutu, Opoku Ware); Fante kept sovereignty by diplomacy and British support. Module 5 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-015 chunk 4 (Boahen, causes, Ewe and western Akan, social change, crafts)
column5: Boahen (GHA V Ch 14): argues that on the Gold Coast the slave trade was the consequence, not the cause, of state building (expansion began 1670s-80s while slaves only mattered economically from 1700-10), against Fage and Clerici who tie Asante and Dahomey to the trade; Ewe lands stayed in about 120 independent dukowo by 1900 and western Akan kept small chiefdoms because migration continued, migrants fled centralisation, Ewe had no gold, ivory or kola surplus and ecological and neighbour interference (Popo, Akwamu, Dahomey, Asante) kept them defensive; population grew in the 16th-17th centuries with American crops (maize) but stagnated or fell in the 18th (Inikori); slaves in Lower Guinea could own property and marry free citizens and origins were not to be divulged among Akan; three new classes: wage-earners, merchant princes (John Kabes of Komenda, John Konny of Ahanta, John Currantee of Anomabo) and mulattos; Dutch and English schools at the castles, SPG missionaries at Cape Coast 1750s, Muslim quarter in Kumasi and Asantehene Osei Kwame (1777-1801) deposed for his attachment to Islam (Wilks); arts: weaving on narrow looms introduced via the Nile valley (Lamb), kente and adanudo matured in the 18th century, adinkra in Brong, cire-perdue gold and brass work by Brong, Denkyira and Asante, gold weights, Asante centralised crafts at Ahwiaa, Bonwire, Tafo, Fumesua and Krofofrom; conclusion that peoples were in full control of their own sovereignty in 1800. Module 5/8 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on the slave-trade-and-state thesis].

column4: ch-021 chunk 1 (Ndaywel e Nziem, Luba and Lunda origins and Luba state)
column5: Ndaywel e Nziem (GHA V Ch 20): Luba and Lunda are two political and cultural systems, not ethnic groups; Upemba Depression finds at Sanga and Katoto are attributed to Luba ancestors with emblems of rule by the 13th century at the latest, but Katoto and Sanga were not direct forerunners; oral chronology cannot be pushed back reliably before 1700 and the Rund state is mentioned only by 1680; copper cross currency about 1300, standardised by 1500, smaller by 1600 and gone after 1700; two interlocked bulopwe principles (sacred kingship and rule through a closed association, Bambudye); Kongolo/Kalala Ilunga epic is traditional and Kongolo may not be authentic; the hunter Cibinda Ilunga and Rweej story for Lunda is a cliche found elsewhere and the Kinguri-to-Angola emigration is a later elaboration (c.1700 at the earliest, Thornton); Rund influences on Luba as much as the reverse (Reefe); Luba kingdom remained small until the eve of the 18th century; Shila state on Lake Mweru and Kanyok subject kingdom; Luba Kasai migrated north in famines; mulopwe 'indivisibility of power'; officials twite, nabanza, lukanga, mwana Mwilamba, mwine Lundu; tribute as mingilu and milambu. Module 6 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED traditions, THIN EVIDENCE for dates].

column4: ch-021 chunk 2 (Ndaywel e Nziem, Luba expansion and the Lunda empire)
column5: Ndaywel e Nziem (GHA V Ch 20): Luba kingdom expanded slowly (Kadilo c.1700 campaign against the Songye failed, real expansion along the Lualaba, succession crisis 1780-1810 when Kanyok broke away, expansion east after 1800), no standing army so Bambudye ideology mattered; he says the inner rationale of the expansion is not understood and trade-route explanations are unconvincing; Lunda: positional succession and perpetual kinship let the empire be run 'as a family', Mwant Yav 'Lord of the Viper', tukwata officials and kazembe generals, mussumba laid out like an army camp; expansion began before 1700 (not the Kinguri emigration story), Musokantanda and Kanongesha went south around 1700 to Ndembu, Kazembe of the Luapula by the second half of the 18th century, de Lacerda visited Kazembe 1798-9, Lunda expansion linked to the Angolan slave trade (Imbangala caravans from the 1670s at the latest), Lunda rejected guns and kept the broadsword, Lunda chiefs on the Kwango by 1750, Chokwe as metallurgists and carvers, Yaka raids caused upheavals and Suku kingdom formed in resistance, Mai Munene on the Kasai; by 1800 Luba and Lunda had structured all the savannah east of the Kwango, with devastation and large-scale slave raiding, bunching of populations along the fifth parallel. Module 6/8 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE for early dates].

column4: ch-026 chunk 1 (Salim, East African coast 1500 and Portuguese intrusion)
column5: Salim (GHA V Ch 25): in 1500 the coast was in its Golden Age (over 100 settlements founded between 1200 and 1500 of about 173 from the 9th to 20th century); Kilwa's prosperity levelling off by 1500, had wrested the Sofala gold trade from Mogadishu in the late 1200s or early 1300s but trade was sea-oriented with no documentary or archaeological evidence for overland routes between Kilwa and the Zambezia gold region, thirteen rulers in 56 years (1442-98), Kilwa population 12 000 per da Gama 1502 (Martin), Malindi walled town of about 3500 people (1000 stone houses, rough estimate); Mombasa 'most powerful city-state' by 1498; Lamu flourished after 1650; Swahili a generic term not used by coastal people until recently, elite claimed Arab or Shirazi origins though of mixed descent, colour of no consequence, ukoo lineage counted; Portuguese: Da Gama 1498 (Mozambique skirmish, Mombasa hostile, Malindi allied), Kilwa made tributary 1502, Zanzibar plundered 1503, Almeida attacked Kilwa 1505 and Mombasa 13 August 1505, Brava 1506, Mombasa razed again 1528 and occupied four months, Kilwa fort abandoned 1512, Sofala garrison dead by 1506 disease; after 1530 Kilwa shifted to ivory; Portuguese went inland to Sena and Tete. Module 6 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE for populations].

column4: ch-026 chunk 2 (Salim, Turks, Zimba, Fort Jesus, Yusuf's revolt)
column5: Salim (GHA V Ch 25): Portuguese had no clear occupation policy and a 'Captain-major of the Sea of Malindi' ran a Malindi factory; Mombasa recovered after destruction, Kilwa almost deserted in 1569 (Monclaro); Ottoman defeat of Mamluks 1517; Mir Ali Bey arrived 1585 and 1588, welcomed by all towns except Malindi; Zimba (originally Lundu's warriors, 1580s) reached Kilwa about 1588 and Mombasa 1589 (the 'cannibalistic Zimba'), Segeju saved Malindi; Malindi took Mombasa with Portuguese help, ending the Shirazi dynasty, Fort Jesus built 1593-4 with 100-man garrison; Pate rising 1603; seventeenth century Oromo pressure and Miji-Kenda dispersal from Shungwaya into fortified makaya; Shungwaya existed (settlement or state) not a mere myth; Sultan Ahmad d.1609, al-Hasan killed, Yusuf baptised in Goa and returned as Dom Jeronimo Chingulia in 1630, seized Fort Jesus 15 August 1631 and massacred nearly all inside, revolt lasted until his death in 1637, Portuguese expedition to Lamu archipelago 1636-7; Dutch blockade of Mozambique 1607; the Zimba/Oromo effects on depopulation hard to gauge. Module 6 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-026 chunk 3 (Salim, Omani conquest of the coast, Kilwa and French slave trade)
column5: Salim (GHA V Ch 25): Omani Ya'rubi imams drove the Portuguese from Muscat by 1650; Pate led resistance, Omani-Pate fleet sacked the Portuguese quarter of Mombasa 1660; Fort Jesus fell on 13 December 1698 after a siege of two and a half years (3000 men on seven ships from March 1696); Portuguese brief return 1728-9, final expulsion November 1729 by Mombasans and Musungulos, Swahili towns responsible for the final expulsion; Portuguese defeat attributed to weak colonial system, incompetent officials, disease, factional struggles; Kilwa-Yao ivory trade grew after the 1690s, setback in early 1700s; Vumba Kuu consolidated with Bantu nicknames for divans; Pate's glory in the 17th-18th century with decline in the late 18th century (Al-Inkishafi poem); Sharifian immigrants from Hadramaut fixed the Shafi'i madhhab; French plantation colonies (Mascarenes after 1735) drove the slave trade, Morice treaty of 1776 for 1000 slaves a year at Kilwa, Mozambique ivory dominance ending by 1785; Omani imam Said bin Ahmad from 1784 imposed an Omani governor on Kilwa, Zanzibar revenue 40 000 piastres in 1796 and nearly 60 000 in 1811; Said bin Sultan (1804-56) later moved his capital to Zanzibar; Portuguese religious impact negligible. Module 6/8 [PROBABLE].

Salim (GHA V Ch 25): Portuguese greed and incompetence caused the decline of the Sofala gold trade; Mombasa resilient, Kilwa recovered late 18th century through the Ile-de-France slave trade but was overshadowed by Kilwa Kivinje; he says ascribing the decline of other towns to Portuguese action is erroneous, human pressures (Oromo, Zimba) and environmental change are more plausible; Pate prospered in the 17th-18th centuries; more research needed on sizes and causes. Module 6 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on cause of decline].

Bhila (GHA V Ch 22): records scarce, Portuguese accounts dominate; Great Zimbabwe culture dated 1200-1450, declining from the mid-15th century with decline tied to falling gold production; Torwa (Butwa) state capitals Khami (founded mid-1400s, burned in the second half of the 17th century) and Danangombe; almost all prestige stone building in Torwa before 1650 and the Rozvi Changamire dynasty (annexed Torwa in the 1690s) built no prestige stone; Mutapa empire by the early 16th century controlled the plateau and part of the Zambezi valley, Manyika, Uteve, Barwe and Danda hived off in the 16th century; Mutapas lost the plateau in the first half of the 18th century, fragmentation from 1629 (Portuguese defeated Mavura Mutapa) to 1917; Mutapa controls: annual rekindling of royal fires, spirit mediums (mhondoro), tribute (skins, ostrich feathers, tusks), labour rent seven days in thirty (Barros), army estimates 100 000, 30 000 regulars (16th century) and 3000 (18th), Portuguese figures 'extremely unreliable'; Portuguese arrived Sofala 1506, regularised trade 1540 with Captain of the Gates, curva tribute (15 000-16 000 cruzados per three years, 'sounds exaggerated'), Gatsi Rusere's 1610 mupeto, Portuguese wars 1569-75 and treaties with Uteve 1575 and Manyika 1573. Module 7 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE on numbers].

column4: ch-023 chunk 2 (Bhila, prazo system and Rozvi origins)
column5: Bhila (GHA V Ch 22): Gatsi Rusere ceded mines by a treaty of 1607 (died 1624), Mavura obtained Portuguese help in 1629 and signed a vassalage treaty (stop curva, expel Swahili-Arab traders, allow Dominicans), baptised as Domingos; prazo system (crown land estates), prazeros with chikunda slave armies (20-30 men on small prazos, thousands on large), Isaacman's Africanisation theory contested, prazo south of the Zambezi 'terras da coroa'; slave exports from Zambezia small by 1752 (300 from Zambezi, 200 from Sofala), Dutch occupation of Angola in the 1640s and Mascarene demand from the 1730s; prazo system decayed in the second half of the 18th century by revolts, famine, slave trade; Rozvi origins speculative: Changamire Dombo I rose 1684-95, rebelled herdsman of the Mutapa, expelled Portuguese from Maungwe 1684, the plateau 1693, Manyika 1695; the name Rozvi from kurozva 'to destroy'; Rozvi capitals Danangombe, Khami and Natetale; Rozvi mwari cult, tribute pyramid, army resembling Shaka's (regiments, crescent formation) as Portuguese described it. Module 7 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Africanisation].

column4: ch-023 chunk 3 (Bhila, Rozvi army and economy)
column5: Bhila (GHA V Ch 22): Rozvi army organised by regiments and the crescent formation like early 19th-century Zulu, Ndebele and Sotho armies (not Roman, as Mudenge noted), but the Rozvi 'invincibility' is exaggerated because Portuguese forces were stretched by the Omani siege of Fort Jesus (1696-98) and prazeros were disunited; Shona economy: finger millet, bulrush millet, sorghum; hoe and shifting agriculture; new crops (rice, yams, sugar cane, fruit, groundnuts) arrived piecemeal and maize only in the 18th century; Nyanga stone terraces used for three or more centuries until 1800, supplementary irrigation probably 18th century; lowveld Hlengwe hunting, gathering, fishing and farming (not solely hunters); contradictory Portuguese reports on improvidence and surplus mean one must heed date and place (Monclaro 1569, Gomes 1648, Barreto 1667), Bhila rejects Beach's 'dangerously static' agriculture, citing innovation and famine-coping methods (mukomondera loans, bartering, pawning). Module 7 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED against Beach's static-agriculture view].

column4: ch-023 chunk 4 (Bhila, cattle, crafts, gold mining and decline)
column5: Bhila (GHA V Ch 22): cattle central to the economy with transhumance between highveld and lowveld since Great Zimbabwe times (13th-15th century) to the late 18th century; tribute of 4000 hornless cows paid by a Butwa ruler to a Mutapa (Alcacova, early 1500s); iron (Njanja hoe makers of Wedza), copper (Duma, 4/5 of 20th-century Zimbabwe copper per a 1952 survey), salt (Middle Save), cloth (cotton on the Zambezi eastern bank); silver never found as a mine, only gold by-product; Portuguese greatly exaggerated gold in the 16th century, alluvial gold collected from rivers and exchanged at the Masekesa feira; mining mainly August-October (dry-season water table, land clearance), fire-setting, village-based alluvial panning by groups of 400 or more; ruling elite appropriated almost 50 per cent of Mutapa gold (estimate), deposits had to be reported on pain of death; decline of seventeenth-century gold production from reaching the water table, low Portuguese prices, and war and famine (Makaranga 'depopulated' in 1683, Chingamire wars), a cause Bhila says historians have ignored. Module 7 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE for the 50 per cent].

column4: ch-023 chunk 5 (Bhila, trade, feiras and the Rozvi-Portuguese relations)
column5: Bhila (GHA V Ch 22): Portuguese trading methods (middlemen with 300-500 carriers, credit and debt slavery) alienated gold-producing peasants and Uteve's king ordered people to stop gold mining by the mid-1600s, so social factors may matter more than geology; Swahili bazaars in the Mutapa empire found about 1514-15, probably dating to the 10th century; Sofala fortress 1506, Sena and Tete 1531, Swahili-Arab traders defeated 1512 then became Portuguese agents; beads (Cambay, caracoes) key trade goods; feiras (Dambarare best, Luanze, Rimuka, Masekesa, Bandire in Uteve) with capitao-mor; after Changamire expelled the Portuguese 1693-5 Zumbo founded 1710 and Masekesa revived 1719; Rozvi raid of 1756-7 confiscated 1000 pastas (800 000 cruzados) after Prince Chirimba seized goods; Rozvi sent forces to protect Zumbo in 1743, 1772 and 1781; Mutapa court kept a 20-man Portuguese garrison in the 18th century with triennial embassies and baptism custom. Module 7 [PROBABLE].

Bhila (GHA V Ch 22): eighteenth-century Mutapa trade declined with the gold rush north of the Zambezi, collapse of gold production and a turn to elephant hunting (ivory harder for rulers to control, sixteenth-century claim of 4000-5000 elephants dying each year); Portuguese penetration eroded the ruling class, vashambadzi African merchant class emerged, regional trade in iron, salt and copper converged with long-distance gold and ivory, peasants exploited by Portuguese mercantile capital. Module 7 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-027 chunk 1 (Webster, Ogot and Chretien, Great Lakes 1500-1800: Nilotic movements and Nyarubanga)
column5: Webster, Ogot and Chretien (GHA V Ch 26): three periods: 1500-1580 successor states to the Bachwezi (Bahinda and Babito) and Eastern Nilotic intrusion; droughts and famines 1580-1680 (the worst: 1588-90, 1601-2, 1613, 1617-21; the Nile at its lowest in 1621, crops normal in only two years, failed totally in eleven), called Nyarubanga in Northern Uganda, the region's largest movement of peoples in a thousand years; state formation and expansion from about 1680 to 1800 with Buganda and Rwanda as the 'super-powers'; Central Sudanic peoples (Lendu, Kebu, Moro, Madi) iron-workers, Luo cradleland Dog Nam broke up about +1000, Eastern Nilotes from about 1490-1571 in three tentative waves (Tekidi regnal list doubtful); Banyoro armies fled during an eclipse in 1520; Pajulu, Kakwa and Kuku culturally Sudanic and linguistically Eastern Nilotic; traditions of estimated half the people dying (the 'half of the population' claim is an estimate by analogy with Egypt), famine pushed survivors toward rivers and lakes, drought destroyed rain-maker leadership and older traditions, so pre-1600 traditions are skeletal and the 'empty land' claims are partly true; the Nyilak story is a stereotype for overthrow of Sudanic leadership. Module 6 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE: dates from regnal lists].

column4: ch-027 chunks 2-3 (Webster, Ogot and Chretien, Luo dispersals, pastoralists and farmers, political forms)
column5: Webster, Ogot and Chretien (GHA V Ch 26): Nyarubanga (1588-1621) scattered the Luo (Pakwac-Pawir as refuge and dispersal centre, three migrations to the Nyanza shore, Padhola, Basoga ruling clans of bushbuck totem; nine Busoga states by 1750 fragmenting to nearly thirty by the late 19th century, father-to-son succession with commoner administrators stable, fraternal succession with princely office-holders prone to civil war), Banyoro 'ravenous hordes' invaded the south, Central Eastern Nilotes (Karimojong, Teso, Jie, Turkana) emerged 1680-1830, Iteso became Eastern Nilotic-speaking and Lango Omiro Luo-speaking, droughts in the 1720s ('Nyamdere'), 1780s and 1830s; they reject the pastoralist-versus-farmer 'watertight compartments' as an oversimplification; Bunyoro lost grazing lands to Buganda between about 1760 and 1783 and Steinhart's tribute-paying peasantry state arose in the 18th century (land not cattle the base, chiefs from Bahima, Bito and Bairu); political forms: Luo hereditary chieftaincy rejected by many Eastern Luo, gerontocratic ritual leadership in Labwor, Lango, Nyakwai, Kumam, military confederacies in Lango, emuron seers; Buganda little class institutionalisation versus Bunyoro and Rwanda, Padibe state moved over 500 miles, Acholi probably fewest cattle by about 1800; Teso average family 3-5 cattle with 10% owning 500-1000 (their figure). Module 6 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE for dates and numbers].

column4: ch-027 chunks 4-5 (Webster, Ogot and Chretien, Bunyoro decline, Buganda rise, southern sources and Hamitic hypothesis)
column5: Webster, Ogot and Chretien (GHA V Ch 26): Bunyoro's crisis after Cwa's death in the Nyarubanga (Winyi II, succession opened to all sons, Isansa c.1733-60 attacked the Wamara Cwezi shrine in Bwera and the 'curse' that Buganda would swallow Bunyoro; Paluo exodus to Acholi, Alur and Busoga; Alur states founded 1670-1850; nadir about 1830 with secession of Toro); Buganda rose through favourable climate (no drought references), water-borne trade, bark cloth, iron ore, no royal clan so any clan could supply the kabaka, Tebandeke (c.1644-74) cut the ritual officers, Mawanda (c.1674-1704) seized Singo, Kyaggwe, Bulamogi and introduced appointed 'king's men', Junju and Kamanya (c.1734-94) expanded, Semakokiro purged princes (mid-18th century in their text), despotism came at the price of rebellions and the 18th century may have been more violent than earlier; southern kingdoms: the 'Hamitic' hypothesis (Speke 1863, Rehse, White Fathers, Lwamgira's Kiziba history) shaped colonial sources; Ruhinda empire dated to about the 15th century if it existed, with versions varying, interpreted as spread of a ruling type; Cwezi religion (Wamara, Mugasha, Ryangombe, Imandwa) older than the dynasties; clans not castes (Rwanda 18 clans each with Hutu, Tutsi and Twa); the Hima/Tutsi lord vs Iru/Hutu serf story is colonial construction. Module 6 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED].

column4: ch-027 chunk 6 (Webster, Ogot and Chretien, southern Great Lakes chronology and Kagera plateau states)
column5: Webster, Ogot and Chretien (GHA V Ch 26): dynastic lists have many variants before the seventeenth century, Kagame's 33-year generation looks more like 27-28; two solar eclipses (probably 1520 at Biharwe and 1792 at Mibambwe Sentabyo's enthronement in Rwanda) anchor dates; the Rwanda mwami exhumed 1968-9 (Van Noten) ascribed to the first half of the 17th century; three Nyoro raids on the south (first half of the 16th century after the 1520 victory, 17th century Kiziba and Karagwe, first half of 18th century Cwa/Kyebambe, defeated by Nyarubamba Kicumbu of Ihangiro and Ntare Kitabanyoro of Karagwe), and the Hinda movement was not Luo in origin against de Heusch; clans of mixed composition (20% of Haya clans, over 10% of Hutu clans, over 50% of Tutsi clans, 90% of Batwa clans in Burundi), so a 'Hamitic conquest' is only another way of describing relations between mainly pastoral and mainly agricultural sectors; Kagera plateau: Karagwe asserted itself from the 17th century, Mpororo (Bashambo dynasty) peaked early 18th century and split after Gahaya Rutindangyezi's death about 50 years later when Ndabarasa of Rwanda occupied the south, Gisaka struck at Rwanda in the 15th and 16th centuries and was beaten by Cyirima Rujugira's warriors, Bugesera linked to Banyiginya, northern Buha kingdoms; Kiziba torn between Bunyoro and Buganda, Kyamutwara's Hinda supremacy from the 17th century. Module 6 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Hamitic and Ruhinda].

column4: ch-027 chunk 7 (Webster, Ogot and Chretien, Rwanda, Burundi and herd-farm relations)
column5: Webster, Ogot and Chretien (GHA V Ch 26): Rwanda tiny from the 14th century, crisis in the 16th (Nyoro invasions, Gisaka held Buganza), Ruganzu Ndori probably founded a new dynasty at the beginning of the 17th century, expansion in the 18th under Cyirima Rujugira and Kigeri Ndabarasa (hereditary standing armies, ubuhake clientship and gikingi land grants, especially under Yuhi Gahindiro at the end of the 18th century), Burundi's Baganwa dynasty founded by Ntare Rushatsi/Rufuku about the end of the 17th century, Rujugira beat Mutaga Senyamwiza in the mid-18th century fixing the Kanyaru border, Burundi and Rwanda each over one million people by the late 19th century; in the east kingdoms fragmented (Kyamutwara, Buzinza, Ihangiro, Bukerebe), in the west they concentrated; relations between herders and tillers not immutable: drought and famine calamities (first half of the 17th century, second half of the 18th) increased herder influence, tribute system favoured pastoral values, American crops (sweet potato, maize, beans, tobacco) possibly 17th century enabling two harvests, the Hima-Iru or Tutsi-Hutu relation developed from local trade to a hierarchy only between the 17th and 19th centuries and colonisation turned it into racial castes; Ganda imperialism on Lake Victoria's west shore in the 19th century. Module 6 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED against the Hamitic and caste reading].

column4: ch-027 chunk 8 (Webster, Ogot and Chretien, consolidation and conclusion)
column5: Webster, Ogot and Chretien (GHA V Ch 26): trade before the 19th century was barter and regional products (Katwe and Uvinza salt, Bazinza and Bashi hoes, raphia bracelets), Indian Ocean shells and beads reached the region in the 17th century (tomb of the Rwandan mwami who died about 1635), copper trade 18th century; Cwezi religion (Ryangombe, Kiranga) offered refuge in the unstable 17th century and monarchs captured it (King of the Imandwa at Rwanda's court from Cyirima Rujugira, ubwiru ritual code, court poetry); Rwanda's exceptional centralisation; conclusion: by the end of the 18th century modern ethnic and linguistic patterns had emerged (Bakiga, Iteso and Lango Omiro completed about 1830), state formation had ended with Rwanda dominant in the south, Bunyoro in decline until Toro and Paluoland seceded in 1830, Buganda pre-eminent in the centre. Module 6 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-025 chunk 1 (Haberland, Horn of Africa overview and the empire about 1500)
column5: Haberland (GHA V Ch 24): the 16th-17th centuries are the most dramatic in the history of north-east Africa: Christian empire collapsed, Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi (Gran) jihad, Oromo expansion, Somali national consciousness and expansion towards the Juba, Susenyos converted to Catholicism in 1630, then 'Age of Princes' from 1700 to 1855 under Tewodros II; about 1500 the empire had a hegemony in north-east Africa, Zara Yaqob (1434-68) cut Islamic states back, Kebra Nagast compiled about 1300 as imperial charter (Solomon, Sheba, Menelik, the Ark at Aksum), Alvares 1520-26 reports order and security, land system (gult grants of tribute rights, ethnic and family land, church land, imperial land), mobile court until Gondar from 1636, no minted coin; Agaw largely assimilated, Haberland says Jewish-practising Agaw were 'extirpated' and survivors became a pariah caste called Falasha (loaded and outdated language: the people call themselves Beta Israel and later work disputes the 'caste' framing); Islamic states Adal, Dawaro, Bale, Ifat, Fatagar, Hadiyya along trade routes; Ethiopia not isolated: monasteries in Jerusalem and Cyprus, monks trained in Egypt, Gibbon's 'slept a thousand years' does not hold. Module 2 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Falasha].

column4: ch-025 chunk 2 (Haberland, Islamic states, Gran's jihad and Oromo)
column5: Haberland (GHA V Ch 24): Islamic states along the trade routes (Adal, Ifat, Fatagar, Argobba, Harar the only ancient city) left Arab influences (irrigation horticulture, cotton, coffee, khat); the 1529 battle of Sembera Kure destroyed the Ethiopian army and elite; Ahmad Gran's armies conquered a province each dry season 1531-1543 (Dawaro, Shoa 1531; Amhara, Lasta 1533; Aksum's Maryam Seyon razed 1533), forced conversions abandoned when armies left; Lebna Dengel died 1540 at Debre Damo; Galawdewos restored the empire; Portuguese volunteer corps of 400 under Cristovao da Gama landed at Massawa in 1541 (their firearms) but Gran also got Turkish artillery from Yemen; imam killed by a Portuguese bullet in February 1543 east of Lake Tana; Haberland says the Portuguese tipped the balance is uncertain; after Galawdewos (1550-9) Muslim states are not named in the chronicles again; Oromo: not the 'barbarians' of Amharic writers, true Ethiopian people from the Bale highlands, migrating from the mid-16th century for pastures, assimilating Hadiyya and others, cattle complex, Borana and Barentu moieties, gada age-grade system (about eighty politically independent groups by the 19th century). Module 2 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Portuguese role].

column4: ch-025 chunk 3 (Haberland, gada, Oromo waves, Somali, empire's survival)
column5: Haberland (GHA V Ch 24): gada system: ten classes of eight years, ruling classes fifth and sixth, abba gada elected, an expedition every eight years; Oromo advanced into areas depopulated by 15 years of war (Mudana after 1530, Kilole after 1538, Bifole after 1546, Meslale after 1554 destroyed much of Adal), learned the horse, Harmufa 1560-70 devastated Angot, Amhara and Bagemder; by Emperor Minas's death a third of the empire permanently Oromo; Muslims disappeared from much of the region except Harar and Awsa; last wave early 17th century into Wallaga and Ilubabor, Gibe states (Gimma, Gumma) absorbed Oromo (kept monarchy not gada), Inariya fell to Limmu Oromo, Kaffa, Sekko and Omotic kingdoms held; Amhara reconquest began about 1700; Somali from the north spread from about the 11th century, in Merka area in the 13th, supported Gran's jihad, Islam an integrating element, absorbed Oromo-related groups and Sab (Digil, Rahanwein), single family tree; empire's struggle 1529-1632 with Portuguese episode and restoration after 1632, Sartsa Dengel (1563-97), Fasiladas fixed capital at Gondar in 1636; the disappearance of eastern Islamic states left Islam no serious threat to the empire for centuries; 1755-1855 'hundred years' anarchy'. Module 2 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-025 chunk 4 (Haberland, Sartsa Dengel, Jesuit mission and Susenyos)
column5: Haberland (GHA V Ch 24): Amir Nur and Galawdewos died in 1559 ending Islamic power in the region; Sartsa Dengel (1563-97) fought Turks, Oromo and the Ethiopian Jews of Semien, Wagara, Dambiya and others (Haberland says the Jewish population was 'practically wiped out', survivors stripped of rights and land and forced into crafts, giving the word Falasha its stigma, framing later contested by scholars), baptism of Inariya and Bosa kings shortly before 1600 as the last imperial expansion; Inariya fell to the Oromo in 1710; the Jesuit mission 1542-1632: Oviedo 1557, Galawdewos's profession of faith, Fremona given to Jesuits, Pedro Paez from 1603 tolerant and impressive, vernacular Amharic theological debate until 1632, works by Enbakom, Bahrey's History of the Galla, annals of Galawdewos, Sartsa Dengel, Susenyos, Walatta Petros (d.1644); Za Dengel excommunicated; Susenyos (1607) turned Catholic in 1622 under Paez's influence, Mendez's re-ordinations, re-baptisms and calendar changes caused revolts, Susenyos abdicated 1632 after a battle ('These were once your loyal subjects'), Fasiladas expelled Jesuits and made a head-money deal with the Turkish governor of Massawa; then deliberate isolation and stagnation, Gondar permanent capital, Yohannes (1667-82) offered Catholics Orthodoxy or exile. Module 2 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Falasha framing].

column4: ch-025 chunk 5 (Haberland, Gondar period and south-west Ethiopia)
column5: Haberland (GHA V Ch 24): Iyasu I (1682-1706) the last great emperor, Gondar period art courtly with Indo-Portuguese builders, rock-church building ended after 1500, book illumination peak about 1500, Durer-style crucifixions in the late 16th century, Fetha Nagast translated from Coptic Arabic had little practical force in Ethiopia (his claim), Zamana Mesafint from about 1755 to 1855; south-west Ethiopia: northern influence created new states (Inariya founded before 1500 by Kaba Seyon from Tigray according to oral tradition, Bosa, Kaffa, Sekko, Wolayta about 1600 by Mika'el from Tigray, Gangero 'Yamgor' tradition), Haberland's thesis that northern monarchy and cavalry transformed small clan groups into states which preserved northern models, with an anecdote of Mika'el throwing cloth and beads as ruse (legend). Module 2 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE: oral tradition].

column4: ch-025 chunk 6 (Haberland, south-west Ethiopia states, social order, crops and Christianity)
column5: Haberland (GHA V Ch 24): southern Ethiopian kingdoms (Gosanaa dynasty's ten dominions, Konta c.1800, Dizi lines from Tigray) replaced equality with ranks, ceremonial courts (Wolayta three ramparts and gates), royal gold and silver rings (Amharic warq and birr), the 'worth complex' of warrior achievement and elected offices with Amharic rank names (dana, geta, ras), artisan castes of low status without land, slaves up to a third of the population in some states (his claim) forming serf-like peasantry; crops arriving from the north after the 14th-15th century (peas, broad beans, chickpeas, onions, garlic, lentils, oilseeds) and American crops (red pepper, maize, tobacco, later pumpkin, sweet potato, potato, tomato); horses for prestige only; plough never adopted in the south; treadle-loom weaving, gold and silver smithing from northern artisans; Christianity's survival as sacred groves named for Christ, Mary and George, descendants of priests (kesiga) performing Mass-like sacrifices, seven-day week, fasting, Meskel as new year, Easter as ritual hunt, after the Oromo barrier cut the south from the abuna. Module 2 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE: oral tradition, 'one third slaves'].

column4: ch-029 chunk 1 (Kent, Madagascar 1500-1800: Antemoro, Zafindraminia, Maroserana)
column5: Kent (GHA V Ch 28): modern Malagasy groups coalesced 1500-1800; by the mid-16th century settlement by overseas newcomers who merged into new populations had ended, early 1600s a political honeycomb of small chiefdoms, then a Sakalava empire in the west, Betsileo and Merina kingdoms, Betsimisaraka confederation in the east in the 18th century; Antemoro (Arabic-script Malagasy scribal tradition, sorabe) settled Matitana between 1509 and 1513 on Portuguese visits (1507, 1508, 1514), earlier idea of Arabian origin disputed, Julien's East African origin supported, their Islam weakened by isolation; Zafikasimambo took power about 1550 and killed Zafindraminia males, Andrianoni Rabesirana (c.1580-1615) and Andriapanolaha (c.1630-60); Zafindraminia (Raminia) predate the 15th century, in Antanosy by about 1500 or 1625 per different writers, failed to unify Antanosy, French Fort Dauphin 1643-74 deflected unification; Maroserana the pan-dynastic family (Mahafaly, Sakalava, Antandroy, Bara) with contradictory origin traditions and the Indian-origin claim of Grandidier doubtful. Module 6 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED origins].

column4: ch-029 chunk 2 (Kent, Maroserana origins and European impact)
column5: Kent (GHA V Ch 28): Maroserana formed in south-western Madagascar about 1550 (not an eastern or Indian origin: Zarabehava of the Antesaka came from Sakalava before 1650 and not earlier than 1620, 'maroserana' meaning disputed), gold imported to the south (volamena sacred) pointing to possible Maroserana-Mwene Mutapa connections he says remain controversial; Maroserana succeeded by alliance with local chiefly families, fortifications, irregular soldiers, redistribution; four early north-west outlets (Vohemar's Iharana on the mainland, Swahili-speaking islet posts in Mahajamba, Boina and Bombetoka) exporting rice and slaves; Portuguese attacked Lulangane 1506; Tingimaro's rising state; Portuguese annual ship for cattle, ambergris, raffia and slaves; Barreto 1667 claim of over 3500 Buques sold a year (Lopes said), Comoros as slave transit (bought at 9-10 piasters sold at 100 in 1614), Luso-Dutch 1641 paper annexation of western Madagascar, Dutch from Mauritius 1639-47 for rice and slaves, English at Saint Augustine Bay with pidgin English, Puritan colony 1645 and Nosy Be 1650 failed. Module 6 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED Maroserana origin][THIN EVIDENCE for slave numbers].

column4: ch-029 chunk 3 (Kent, Fort Dauphin, Mascarenes, Mahafaly and Sakalava states)
column5: Kent (GHA V Ch 28): English pirates and traders exported Malagasy slaves to Barbados and Jamaica (half of Barbados's 32 473 slaves around 1700 from Madagascar), faulty guns traded; Fort Dauphin 1643-74, Flacourt governor 1648-58, 2000 colonists 1667, delayed Antanosy unification; Mascarenes (Bourbon 10 338 slaves and 2358 whites in 1744; Mauritius ex-Dutch 1710, occupied 1715-21; over 80% slaves in 1797) took most Malagasy slaves 1664-1766 then Africans; Mahafaly (four kingdoms from the 1650s, Linta c.1670, Onilahy c.1750), Sakalava Menabe founded by Andriandahifotsy (died about 1685, army of 12 000 in the early 1670s seen by a French trader), Iboina founded by Tsimanatona in the 1690s with less than 1000 warriors, Sakalava origin from the Bambala coast (Bantu-speaking Cafres) not a linguistic problem, dady ancestor cult, Iboina at its height under Andrianihanarivo (d.1752), royal court at Marovoay. Module 6 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE army numbers].

column4: ch-029 chunk 4 (Kent, Sakalava government, Antankara, Betsileo, early Merina)
column5: Kent (GHA V Ch 28): Iboina under Queen Ravahiny (c.1767-1808) prosperous but declining; Sakalava kingdoms 'despotic and regal' with royal moasy, six-elder council, dady relics; Tsimihety formed from refugees of the slave wars and refused Maroserana rule; Antankara royal line from Kazobe, Andriantsirotso (c.1697-1710 or 1710-c.1750) brought the crescent-and-star flag; Betsileo named from Besilau who opposed Menabe in the 1670s, four states (Arindrano, Isandra, Lalangina, Manandriana), kingdoms doubtful before the 1650s, 3000 flintlocks for 3000 slaves, Betsileo foremost rice growers, Andriamanalina I (to 1790) unified Isandra and parts of others; Merina: Ralambo (about 1610-1640) first state organisation, royal bath fandroana, sampy amulets, head tax and standing army; Andriamanelo's iron spears and fortification at Alasora; Andrianjaka founded Antananarivo with firearms from west-coast traders; irrigated rice gave an early economic base, he is dated per tradition. Module 6 [PROBABLE][TRADITIONAL DATE].

column4: ch-029 chunk 5 (Kent, Imerina, interior and Betsimisaraka)
column5: Kent (GHA V Ch 28): Andriamasinavalona (c. to about 1750) divided Imerina into four kingdoms; Andrianampoinimerina (Ramboasalama, from about 1777-8) reunified Imerina, took Antananarivo in 1797, sent envoys offering vassalage, ended tribute to the Sakalava, built the base for the 19th century Merina empire (his legendary harshness reported by tradition); Sihanaka and Bezanozano as trade intermediaries and slavers (Imerina slaves reaching the coast), no central authority, Martin 1667 found fortified stone-walled Sihanaka villages; Tanala-Ikongo Zafirambo dynasty from Rambo (an Antemoro exile) first mentioned 1668; Bara pastoralists emerged on the Ihosy, Zafimanely kinglets after about 1650 raiding each other's cattle; Betsimisaraka confederation founded by Ratsimilahoe (born of an English pirate father, recaptured Fenerive 1712, elected mpanjaka-be, died 1754) holding a loose confederation, later rulers slavers (Iavy the biggest), eastern Madagascar in the second half of the 18th century 'resembled Angola in its slaving tragedies'; Antesaka founded from the west by Andriamandresi's line (Zarabehava) by the 1650s, Antefasy possibly 1670s. Module 6 [PROBABLE][TRADITIONAL DATE].

column4: ch-029 chunk 6 (Kent, Antanosy decline, Antandroy and the Comoros)
column5: Kent (GHA V Ch 28): of about 4000 settlers sent to Fort Dauphin by 1674 two-thirds died; a Martinique pirate was 'king' there in 1698; Count of Modave found 35 rulers in Antanosy 1767-70 fighting for slaves and cattle, the most powerful ruling fewer than 3000 villagers, Antanosy by then 'poorest and saddest'; Antandroy 'Zafimanara confederation' fragile; the Comoros settled by Bantu-speaking mainlanders, Islam via Afro-Shirazi, bedja and fani chiefs and stone building, earliest mosque at Chingoni on Mayotte with carved date read 944 AH (1566) or 844 AH (1441) by different authors, Sultanic period started 1506 or earlier than 1400, Hasan founder of the Anjouan dynasty (queen supreme in 1599-1602), Moheli sultan fluent in Portuguese in 1602 who knew charts, Grande Comore divided among ten lords in 1614, Msamudu mosque 1670, pirates 1680-1720 sacked Comorean towns, Comoreans middlemen and slave raiders; Kent warns for the Comoros that no professional history exists before the 19th century. Module 6 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-029 chunk 7 (Kent, Anjouan revolt and the Mascarenes)
column5: Kent (GHA V Ch 28): Anjouan under Sultan Ahmad (from 1736, over 40 years) faced the 1775 revolt of the Wamatsaha led by Tumpa demanding equality, put down with British marines; Sakalava and Betsimisaraka outrigger raids on the Comoros for slaves ended by about 1825; Mayotte became Malagasy-speaking after Sakalava flight from Iboina; Mascarenes uninhabited until Europeans: Dutch at Mauritius from 1638 to 1710, Reunion settled 1646 and 1654 from Fort Dauphin, Mauritius colonised from Reunion by 1721, royal administration 1767, populations about 2000 around 1710 (a third slaves), about 6000-8000 by mid-century, and 120 000 including about 94 000 slaves by the end of the 1700s, Malagasy slaves stopped being bought in part because of marronage fear, first sugar mill under Mahe de Labourdonnais (1735-46), coffee from 1715 at Reunion. Module 6/8 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-022 chunk 1 (Phiri, Kalinga and Bhila, northern Zambezia-Lake Malawi before 1500 and Maravi origins)
column5: Phiri, Kalinga and Bhila (GHA V Ch 21): region from the Zambezi to the Songwe and Ruvuma; iron-using farmers from about +300 (Mwavarambo and Kapeni pottery), modern Bantu-speaking settlement after about +1200 (Mawudzu, Luangwa pottery); before 1500 mostly stateless small chieftaincies with shared religion (Nyau, Chisumphe, Chikangombe rain cults); the Maravi (from Luba area of south-east Zaire) arrived by radiocarbon dates 1420-1480 on their sites, Newitt thinks the early 16th century, they built a confederation over eastern Zambia, central and southern Malawi and northern Mozambique by the early 17th century, with the state process 'not clearly understood' (Hamilton's invasion thesis vs Roberts's imported techniques and ideas vs demographic and ecological explanations); Ngulube immigrants founded Lambya, Ngonde, Chifungwe, Sukwa late in the 16th century. Module 7 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Maravi state formation].

column4: ch-022 chunk 2 (Phiri et al., Maravi state and expansion)
column5: Phiri, Kalinga and Bhila (GHA V Ch 21): four hypotheses on Maravi state formation (invasion with chiefly symbols, imported ideas and techniques, demography and soil, ivory trade control via the Shire-Zambezi, conflict and compromise with proto-Chewa 'owners of the soil'); Kalonga Chidzonzi's capital at Manthimba and Mankhamba the religious centre, mlira cult and bush burning, officials khombe, mkomba, mgawi; Portuguese 1624 report of Manthimba as dense and commercial; expansion in the last quarter of the 16th century by sending junior Phiri heads (Mpinganjila, Nyangu, Changamire, Chauma, Chinsamba) and distant kin Kaphwiti and Lundu to the Lower Shire; Lundu ruled the Lower Shire by 1572, spearheaded eastward expansion into Lolo and Makua from about 1560, Lundu's warriors perhaps the Zimba who defeated the Portuguese at Sena in 1592 then sacked Kilwa and Mombasa until beaten at Malindi (Schoffeleers thinks Zimba originated south of the Zambezi), Lundu conquered state 'Bororo', Mbona cult at Khulubvi; Kalonga-Lundu rivalry stalled eastward growth in the 1620s-30s; Undi founded a kingdom on the Kapoche in the mid-17th century, influence over Nsenga by trade and famine relief as well as force (extent debated); Chulu, Kaluluma, Kanyenda and Kabunduli moved into Tumbuka country creating the Tonga. Module 7 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Zimba and Maravi origins].

column4: ch-022 chunk 3 (Phiri et al., Maravi golden age, Ngulube states, decline)
column5: Phiri, Kalinga and Bhila (GHA V Ch 21): seventeenth century a Maravi 'golden age' with Portuguese cooperation (4000 Maravi warriors to Tete in 1608 for Gatsi Rusere's campaign, Lundu aid 1614 and 1635, Kalonga's thousands in 1623) though Portuguese called the Maravi 'very bad neighbours'; Ngulube immigrants from the north-east founded Ulambya, Kameme, Misuku, Ungonde (Kyungu from about 1600, Mbande hill, Simbowe trade chief, glass beads, porcelain and conus shells in 15th-16th century excavations) with regnal lists giving minimum nine to maximum twelve dynastic generations (so dates approximate); Kyungu killed by smothering (makambala), Kasyombe c.1750 ended it, Mwangonde (c.1785-1839); Maravi decline from the mid-18th century by secessions from the Kalonga, Lundu and Undi, causes unclear, Portuguese gold rush of the 1740s-50s and Makewana's shrine at Msinja. Module 7 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE regnal list dates].

column4: ch-022 chunk 4 (Phiri et al., Maravi decline, prazos, ivory and slave trades)
column5: Phiri, Kalinga and Bhila (GHA V Ch 21): Maravi decline blamed on Makewana's defection from Kalonga and Undi, Makua-Lolo ethnic consciousness and war on the Portuguese from 1749 using French and Brazilian guns; prazos north of the Zambezi (Chikunda retainers), Portuguese gold at Undi's capital c.1740-1780s about 100 kg (3500 oz) a year; Yao trade rose in the late 17th-early 18th century (Chisi ironsmiths, Kilwa ivory market 1635-1698, then Mossuril), Bisa traders from Kazembe, ivory replaced by slaves late 18th century (Kilwa slave trade from the 1770s, exports to Reunion and Bourbon 1780s), 'the eighteenth century is the ivory century and the nineteenth the slave century', Tumbuka linked to long-distance trade in the first decades of the 18th century by Balowoka (Gondwe, Katumbi). Module 7/8 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE gold weights].

column4: ch-022 chunk 5 (Phiri et al., Tumbuka trader-chiefs and conclusion)
column5: Phiri, Kalinga and Bhila (GHA V Ch 21): in the 18th century the Tumbuka area was dominated by ivory hunters then traders whose wealth became political authority (Gondwe of Nkamanga, Katumbi at Hewe, Mwaheng at Henga with salt, Mankhambira on the lakeshore from the 1720s), turbans as symbols of authority, Gondwe's trade monopoly by 1800; the northern states stayed outside long-distance trade until the nineteenth century; the region's historical ages start about 1400 in the south (Maravi) and about 1600 in the north (Ngulube); nineteenth-century themes: ivory to slaves, Yao chiefdoms, Nguni, Swahili, Kololo. Module 7 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-024 chunk 1 (Denoon, southern Africa 1500-1800: San, Khoi, Nguni)
column5: Denoon (GHA V Ch 23): before 1652 southern Africa's external links were sporadic, ships watered at the Cape; Cape Town a 'seaward-looking' dependency; hunter-gatherers (San) and herders (Khoi) co-existed with cultivators and could revert between ways of life, transitions not 'evolutionary'; Elphick's view that San groups acquired stock before 1500 and became Khoi; Xhosa-Khoi interpenetration (Gonaqua, Gqunukhwebe, Ntinde incorporated into Xhosa society), so Khoi territory was not consistently contracting in earlier centuries; the question 'when was the mass migration from the north' was misconceived and driven by settlers' land legitimation; stable settlement and short moves; Nguni and Sotho late Iron Age by 1500; maize adopted in the 18th century, perhaps raising stock; Peires estimates no more than 100 000 Xhosa-speakers by 1800 so no serious land pressure; chiefs' power limited by commoners until the end of the 1700s. Module 7 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED against the 'great migration' model].

column4: ch-024 chunk 2 (Denoon, Portuguese, Dutch Cape, frontier societies)
column5: Denoon (GHA V Ch 23): Portuguese Mozambique a feudal seaborne empire of middlemen (prazos as feudal manors; 'merchant capitalism without capital, colonization without colonists'); Dutch East India Company founded 1602, Cape garrison settlement from 1652 under van Riebeeck as provisioning post, pastoral capitalism did not articulate with other modes but obliterated Khoi and San society, slaves imported, 150 years later over 20 000 free burghers and over 25 000 slaves; frontier new societies (Kora, Griqua, Nama 1730-1780s, gun-based cattle raiding, leaders like Bloem and the Kok family), Xhosa succession rivalries after Phalo's death in 1775 (Rharhabe, Gcaleka, Ndlambe and Ngqika after 1782), eastern frontier conflict of the 1790s, 1795 burgher republics of Swellendam and Graaff-Reinet, Khoi dispossession and Hottentot Corps 1795. Module 7 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-024 chunk 3 (Denoon, Khoi revolt and British Cape)
