column5: Denoon (GHA V Ch 23): British seized the Cape in 1795, burgher republics suppressed, Khoi revolt of 1799 (Klaas Stuurman) pacified by land grants, Cape Town about 15 000 people, colony about 22 000 Christians, 14 000 Khoi and San and 25 000 slaves with caste-like access to land; northern Nguni confederacies leading to the Zulu state arose independently of Cape events; commercial pastoralism the lasting transforming force. Module 7 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-013 chunk 1 (Izard and Ki-Zerbo, Bambara kingdoms of Segu and Kaarta)
column5: Izard and Ki-Zerbo (GHA V Ch 12): four poles emerged after Gao's fall in 1591: Bambara kingdoms of Segu and Kaarta, Mossi kingdoms, Kong and Gwiriko, Gulmance kingdoms; they reject 'tribalised power' and say traditions of Mali and Gao continued on a smaller scale; Bambara origins in oral traditions with differing succession orders and reign lengths (they prefer Raffenel and Tauxier's chronology), Tauxier's racist claim that Bambara could never found kingdoms quoted and rejected; Bambara 'Ban-ma-na refusal of the master'; Mamari Kulibali (Biton, 1712-55) rose through the ton age-association, killed elders of Donkouna and Banankoro, held 1751 Niani tribute and pashas' tribute, Denkoro (1755-7) executed, Ngolo Diarra (1766-90) restored monarchy and moved to Segu-Sikoro, Monson Diarra (1792-1808); Kaarta (Massasi) under Sunsan, Massa, Benefali (c.1710-45), Fulakoro captured, Sira Bo Kulibali (1761-80) at Guemu; ton-dyon captives of the ton formed the army and aristocracy, faama title; state formed in miniature from an age-association in a few decades. Module 4 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE on dates].

column4: ch-013 chunk 2 (Izard and Ki-Zerbo, Segu army and the Mossi kingdoms)
column5: Izard and Ki-Zerbo (GHA V Ch 12): Segu faama's power became autocratic as the ton assemblies weakened, senate of forty, army of sofa, kini-n-bolo and numa-n-bolo with ton-dyon officers, booty shares (a quarter each to king, religious chiefs, Somono and troops), Somono fishermen and foroba-fulaw as state services, Kaarta more autocratic and homogeneous; Mossi: Wubri about 1495, Yadega about 1540 (Yatenga) as in volume IV, Mogo Naaba title; Dagomba under Na Nyaghse (1460-1500), Gonja founded in the second half of the 16th century by a Mande chief, Gonja's Lata Jakpa (1622/3-1666/7) killed Na Dariziegu, Dagomba beat Gonja at Tunuma 1713, Asante under Opoku Ware compelled Dagomba in 1744 to send 2000 prisoners a year to Kumasi (an 'enormous number'), Dagomba became a channel of Asante influence and man-hunting; Ouagadougou: Kumdumye put sons in Yako, Tema, Mane, Konkistenga and Bussuma, Kuda moved to Sapone, Fulbe usurper Moatiba (1729-37) erased from lists, Warga (1737-44) legislator who organised royal servants, capitalised women (napogsyure) and instituted castration (the authors doubt he did all attributed to him). Module 4/5 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE: dates from king lists].

column4: ch-013 chunk 3 (Izard and Ki-Zerbo, Yatenga and Mossi structure)
column5: Izard and Ki-Zerbo (GHA V Ch 12): Mossi kingdoms are composite formations resulting from conquest by warriors called Mossi plus intermarriage and slow peasant settlement rather than 'waves of horsemen'; Yatenga under Naaba Kango (1754-87) returned from Segu in 1757 with Bambara riflemen, refused the ringu enthronement, founded Ouahigouya about 1780, centralised power through royal servants (first guns in Yatenga probably under Piiyo), massacred Bambara mercenaries; Naaba Zombre (1744-84), Kom (1784-91) first to spread Muslim influence; nakombse/take/naaba distinction, five-generation royal lineage, tasobnamba war-chiefs, nesomba court officers (Togo, Balum, Weranga, Bin-Naaba), tengsoba earth priests, naaba versus 'sons of the land', Wende King-God and Napaga Tenga Queen-Land, annual ritual cycle (filiga, napusum, bega); Fulbe settled in Yatenga since the 17th century, Silmi-Mossi from Tema in the 18th century. Module 4/5 [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-013 chunk 4 (Izard and Ki-Zerbo, Gulma, Borgu and non-centralised peoples)
column5: Izard and Ki-Zerbo (GHA V Ch 12): Gulma (Gurma) states of the Buricimba (Bemba) built over Dogon, Tindamba, Wobba and Kurumba, early centre Lompotangu, Gulmance state beginnings in the 14th-15th century at the earliest (Madiega), peak about 1750, Nungu founded by Yendabri in the mid-1700s, Tyokosi Mande mercenaries expelled; Jaba and Lompo not the Mossi Na Gbewa descendants (Mossi claims of link are late reconstructions at the Mogo-Naaba's court, colonial-era); Borgu (Wasangari from Busa, Nikki, Bariba kingdoms); non-centralised peoples: reject 'stateless' and 'acephalous' labels, Mossi are a mixture ('Moaga' = mixed per Delobsom), peasant penetration more decisive than horsemen, Kumdumye died trying to reach Boromo, Red Volta became the western border; Gurunsi is not a self-name but an outsider term; Bwaba and Do religion. Module 4/5 [PROBABLE][CONTESTED on Mossi-Gulmance links].

column4: ch-013 chunk 5 (Izard and Ki-Zerbo, Kong, Gwiriko, economy, slavery)
column5: Izard and Ki-Zerbo (GHA V Ch 12): Samo (Sana) confederations resisted Mossi; Bisa; Juula traders pushed south as the slave and gun trade grew on the Guinea coast from the 16th century, Begho destroyed at the end of the 17th century and Bonduku founded by refugees in Bron kingdom, Buna Kulango kingdom modelled on Dagomba; Senufo egalitarian farmers and artists whose centralised states came only in the 19th century; Kong under Sekou Wattara (to 1740) with Senufo troops under Juula officers reached Sofara and was beaten by Biton Kulibali, then split between Muslim Salama Juula traders and non-Muslim Sohondji warriors; Gwiriko founded by Famaghan Wattara around Bobo-Dioulasso (rulers Kere Massa 1742-9, Magan Oule 1749-1809), domination mainly economic; Black Volta gold high production from the mid-18th century with Bobo-Juula (Kietegha); Mossi country near monoculture of millet with two bad and two very bad years per decade; Yarse traders supplanted Marase, cowrie, cubit of cotton strip; blacksmiths; Naaba Kango's capital as a salt depot; slave hierarchy in the Bambara system (ton-dyon, foroba-dyon, san'dyon, woloso who could not be sold and could inherit); ruling families kept the memory of servile ancestry (Ngolo Diarra). Module 4/8 [PROBABLE][THIN EVIDENCE for gold timing].

column4: ch-013 chunk 6 (Izard and Ki-Zerbo, Islam and conclusion)
column5: Izard and Ki-Zerbo (GHA V Ch 12): the idea that Bambara and Mossi were barriers to Islam is simplistic: Bambara kings combined marabouts with their own cults (Biton paid zakat to Jenne marabouts), Islam in the Volta basin came from the south and west (Juula along the Black Volta, Bobo-Dioulasso, Gonja Mande founders; Dagomba Na Zangina first Dagomba king converted early 18th century, Mamprusi, Naaba Dulugu c.1796-c.1825 converted formally and built the first mosque in Ouagadougou), Yatenga stayed closed to Islam until colonisation despite Fulbe and Yarse Muslims; Kong and Bobo had militant Islam, Gulmanceba held to tradition until the Liptako jihad; conclusion: state-building phase, states multi-ethnic not 'ethnic states', vulnerable for lack of written administration, internal contradictions (princes vs commoner ministers, clan vs ton vs territorial state), the shadow of the slave trade and external markets, yet people built states 'with their own African means'. Module 4/5 [PROBABLE].

Interior of Kenya and Tanzania 1500-1800: no record of Arab or Swahili penetration of the interior before 1700; no imported objects at interior sites north of the Zambezi before 1600 (Oliver). Interior sat apart from coast until about 1800.

Famine the main challenge (Iliffe); crop variety as insurance; maize, groundnuts, sweet potato and cassava introduced after 1500, routes of spread poorly known; cattle dispersed by loans and bridewealth to spread risk.
Internal trade: iron (Ha, Zinza), salt (Uvinza springs exploited since about AD 1000, Ugogo, Eyasi), pots, Kikuyu-Kamba-Maasai exchange; Miji-Kenda middlemen by 1750 replaced by Kamba by mid-1700s.

Two political types: decentralised (Kikuyu, Kamba, Maasai, Kalenjin) and centralising (Shambaa, Pare, Sukuma, Nyamwezi); ntemi chiefships; Kimambo rejects diffusionist common-origin theory (Oliver and Fage); Nyamwezi centralised only in 19th century trade; Fipa Milansi/Twa; Luo gweng and buch piny; Nandi orkoiyot.

Conclusion says technical gap with Europe was great by 1800 and that Africa 'had fallen far behind'; a framing the course should present as the author's view, not a fact established by the chapter's evidence.

Senegambia: Portuguese trade from 1445 (Arguin) diverted routes to the coast; Jolof confederacy broke up in the 16th century (Waalo, Kayor, Bawol, Siin, Salum split; Denyanke Futa Toro dominant); Kaabu replaced Mali in the Southern Rivers; leather trade 150,000 hides in 1660; Rodney: at least 5,000 slaves a year from the Southern Rivers 1562-1640.
Barry says Curtin underestimates Senegambia's share of the Atlantic slave trade (Curtin: under 10 per cent after 1640); admits no reliable statistics. A disagreement to teach as such.

Marabout War (Tubenan) 1673-77 under Nasir al-Din: opposed slave trade and aristocratic pillage, defeated with French aid in 1677; Nasir al-Din died 1674; Trarza and Brakna emirates survived. Barry's interpretation attacked by Curtin; Barry notes a Waalo error in his earlier book (fn 16).

Ceddo regimes: Lat Sukaabe Fall (1695-1720) of Kayor-Bawol with royal monopoly on arms and slaves; Waalo and the French and English; English took 8,000+ slaves in Waalo in under six months in 1775; Samba Gelaajo Jeegi of Futa Toro (1725-31); Ormans from Morocco about 5,000 (Saint-Robert).

Muslim revolutions: Bundu (Maalik Sy about 1690), Futa Jallon (Karamokho Alfa, 1725 per Rodney, Talansan), Futa Toro (Sulayman Baal and Abd al-Qadir 1776; Bungoy defeat 1790-91); Futa Jallon runde slave villages, slave revolts, Fulfulde literature; Barry says revolution not a Fulbe-v-Jallonke ethnic war and that the new regimes later joined the slave trade.

Conclusion's claims that Europe was integrating Senegambia into capitalism and that theocracies lost revolutionary character just as abolition neared are Barry's thesis; the chapter gives no figures for finance capital.

Cameroon grasslands, Uele and Ubangi 1500-1800: sources thin; Tikar, Bamum (Nchare, ten kings to Kuotu, 10-12,000 people by end of 18th c, Tardits revised the history), Bamileke; Fulbe pressure from mid-18th c or earlier; Zande/Mangbetu formed by elite conquest not mass migration (Vungara, Bandia).

Coast of Gabon and Cameroon: Pacheco Pereira about 1505 says coast densely populated; Duala king Mulobe about 1650; Loango kingdom well established by 1500, origins disputed (from Kongo or internal Vili); king's ritual functions, sacred fire, rain festival; palm-cloth currency.

Atlantic trade on the Loango coast: Sao Tome entrepot from 1500; massive expansion about 1660; Loango slave exports 100 a year about 1639, 12,500 a year 1762-78, 13-14,000 a year 1780-90, ending almost by 1780 as Loango lost importance to Cabinda and Malemba; Teke (Monteques) and Bubangi (Quibangues) among exports; palm-cloth 6-7,000 pieces a year to Luanda.

Rodney (technological stagnation, ruin of local metalwork and textiles) against Curtin (three transatlantic migrations may balance out); M'Bokolo says debate remains open. American crops (maize, cassava, groundnuts, beans, tobacco) spread over about two and a half centuries from about 1600; Vansina calls it an agricultural revolution; M'Bokolo doubts it raised population.

Congo river trade (Harms, Vansina): Malebo Pool markets, Kingabwa pottery 1450-1650, camwood and copper; three stages of Atlantic trade (to about 1560 Kongo; 1560-1750 Pool-Loango axis; 1750-1850 basin main supplier); slaves from Lulonga, Alima, Boma, Ubangi; ivory second until reversal after 1830; segmented trade; Bobangi trading firms; Tio decentralised; no capitalism.

Loango coast slave export figures and shipping routes ('small route' and 'great route'); captains preferred Loango slaves; Cameroon trade busiest about 1750 (Dutch); figures for Cameroon and Gabon unquantified.

Africans in Iberia, England, France, Venice: Portugal imported est. 700-900 slaves a year 1450-1500; est. 100,000 slaves in Portugal and Madeira by early 1600s; papal bulls 1454 and 1456; Granville Sharp, Somerset case 1772 (Mansfield did not abolish slavery), est. 15,000 Africans in England.

Americas: Africans with explorers (Estevanico); Jamestown 1619; slavery established in English North America by 1660; Barbados 1627, Jamaica 1655; Maroon War Jamaica 1725 and 1739 treaty with Cudjoe; Palmares 1605-95 est. 20,000; Guyana risings 1763-4; Cato's Rebellion 1739; Islam in Bahia.

Diaspora institutions and voices: Sierra Leone 1787 (over 400), Paul Cuffee 1814 (38), Free African Society 1787, Prince Hall, Phillis Wheatley, Equiano (Harris says born Benin 1745), Banneker, Sancho, Cugoano; San Domingo about 500,000 slaves, 24,000 free coloured, 32,000 settlers; Toussaint; Harris says Toussaint defeated Napoleon's army within five years, loose.

Asia: slave trade to Asia older than Atlantic; Oman took Kilwa 1784 and Zanzibar 1785; Mascarenes about 160,000 imported 1670-1810, Bourbon 53,726 in 1808; Habshi/Siddi in India: Bengal 1486-93 (30,000 army), Gujarat, Janjira, Malik Ambar of Ahmadnagar 1602-26; Gannibal bought in Constantinople 1696; Black Jews of Cochin.

Harris attributes the Asiento do Negros of 1518 to Charles I of Portugal (Charles I was king of Spain) and says Alexandre Dumas was born in the nineteenth century (the plate gives General Dumas 1762-1806); sloppy; do not repeat.

Ottoman conquest of Egypt: Marj Dabiq 24/08/1516, Raydaniyya 23/01/1517 (Tumanbay last Mamluk sultan); causes: Ottoman technical superiority, defection of Khayr Bey, Mamluk economic weakness after Portuguese took spice trade; Khayr Bey governed to 1522.

Kanun Name after 1524 revolt of Ahmad Pasha: wali, Diwan, six then seven odjaks, 14 districts, mukata'at then iltizam by about 1658; hazine sent to Istanbul from 1525 (agreed 400,000 guldens); cadastral survey not complete until 1576, full register 1608.

Ottoman reach in the Red Sea: Aden 1538, Say fortress in Nubia, Massawa and Zeila 1557 (Ozdemir Pasha), province of Habesh, Berberistan; Upper Egypt province 1583; coffee replaced spices in transit trade; Suez canal idea of 1560s dropped.

Internal conflict: spahi revolts 1598-1609; beys' coup 1631; Fakariyya v Qasimiyya; riots 1678, 1687, 1695; famine 1695; protection charges; coffee export crisis about 1710; 1711 siege; Cairo 300,000 (peak 250,000 in 14th c); odjaks integrated by intermarriage.

Duumvirs 1744-54, Kazdughliyya to 1798; Ali Bey al-Kabir 1760-72 (Bulut Kapan, minted coins, Syria with Russian fleet contact 1770), Muhammad Bey Abu al-Dhahab to 1775; Murad and Ibrahim 1778-91; Hasan Pasha 1786-87 failed; Napoleon 1798; Vesely: Egypt did not reach a bourgeois stage, calls it late feudalism with a caveat.

Culture: Cairo lost its role as centre of Sunni world; Arabic literature in popular forms (Hazz al-quhuf 1787); Dervish orders; no printing press in Egypt in the 18th c though Istanbul printed from 1729; Ottoman mosques with local elements.

column4: vol V ch 7 (Hasan and Ogot) p.171-3
column5: Sudan 1500-1800: the north-south frontier was shifting and a wide zone, not fixed; Arabization more cultural than ethnic; authors say racial 'Arab north, African south' framing came from colonial writers and post-Mahdiyya period.

Abdallabi (Arab confederacy under Abdallah Jammaa conquered Alwa/Soba late 15th c, Arab alone not Funj) defeated by Funj at Arbaji 1504; Funj sultanate at Sennar, origins disputed (Shilluk per Bruce, Umayyad claim in tradition); Badi II Abu Dikn 1644-1718 golden age; Badi IV 1721-62; Abu Likaylik deposed him 1762, Hamaj regents; Shilluk and Funj.
Ottoman Berberistan: Ozdemir, Say fortress, Bosnian garrisons, frontier at Hannik about 1622; Suakin, Massawa 1557 province of Habes; Funj-Ethiopian wars 1618-19 and 1744 (Dindera, Funj victory).

Islam and trade: Maliki law, Qadiriyya introduced 1577, Shadhiliyya/Majdhubiyya; Sudan Road and Forty-Days Road (Darb al-Arbain); Sennar 'greatest trading city' 1701 (Krump); slave trade and slave armies in Funj and Fur.

Fur sultanate: Dali, Tunjur, Kayra dynasty from about 1640 (Sulayman Solongdungu), Ahmad Bukr 1682-1722, Kurkwa slave army, Muhammad Tayrab, Abd al-Rahman al-Rashid founded al-Fashir; Kayra 1640-1874.

Southern Sudan: Nilotic expansion; Shilluk kingdom (Nyikang about 1490-1517, Fashoda founded by Tugo 1690-1710, Reth Dhokoth, famine 1684, canoes control White Nile until Turco-Egyptian shipyard 1826); Dinka pressure from about 1630; Bahr al-Ghazal peoples, tradition shallow; Zande conquest beginning 1800.

Maghrib crisis in the early 16th c: population estimated 3 to 6 million after 14th-15th c epidemics; nomad pressure; Zayyanids (Tlemcen) and Hafsids (Tunis) declining; Cherif attributes decline to structural causes and rejects blaming the Hilalians alone.

Spanish presidios 1505-74 (Oran 1509, Tripoli 1510-51, Goulette 1535-74); Barbarossa brothers; Ottoman conquest: Tripoli 1551, Kairouan 1557, Djerba 1558, Tunis 1569 and 1574; Tlemcen fell 1551-4; regencies never fully integrated, no regular tribute; Janissaries.

Society under the regencies: kabila and saff confederations, makhzen v siba; Berber refuge zones; kulughli; Tunis and Tripoli open to locals while Algiers exclusive (kulughli excluded about 1630-80); Muradite beys Tunis (to 1702), Karamanli Tripoli 1711, Algiers deys 1671: eleven deys 1671-1710.

Privateering: Algiers about 80 vessels, Tunis 30-40 about 1610-30; zenith in first half of 17th c, decline from 1680s; European treaties from 1670s-80s, import duties 3 per cent for English then French (unequal treaties); cereals, leather (Leghorn Jews monopoly in Tunis); trans-Saharan trade through Tripoli.

18th century: Husayn b. Ali bey of Tunis 1705; Ali Pasha revolt 1728; peace 1762-1815 under Ali Bey 1759-82 and Hammuda Pasha 1782-1814; Algiers dey Muhammad b. Uthman 1766-91, Kabyle revolt 1767-71, French conquest 1830; Tripoli Karamanli 1711-1835, Ottoman return May 1835; 1784-5 plague; Cherif: conclusion that the Ottoman solution brought stagnation and iron rule.

Morocco: Sa'did dynasty proclaimed 1511 (al-Qa'im); Agadir taken 1541-2 after Portuguese sugar export monopoly; Safi and Azemmur evacuated 1542; Muhammad al-Shaykh enters Fez 13/09/1554, assassinated 1557 by an agent of the Ottomans; al-Ghalib to 1574; trade with Rouen merchants 1570.

Battle of the Three Kings (Wadi al-Makhazin) 04/08/1578: Don Sebastian, Abd al-Malik died during the battle, Ahmad al-Mansur; about 14,000 Christian prisoners by tradition; ransoms enriched al-Mansur (al-Dhahabi), per Levi-Provencal more than the Sudan conquest; El Fasi says the letters between Abd al-Malik and Sebastian are not in European documents.
Al-Mansur's Sudanese expedition: ulama and nearly everyone opposed it as war on Muslims (Terrasse), he overrode them; died 1603; half a century of succession wars; Arzila 1589.
Alawite dynasty from 1640 (Mawlay al-Sharif/Muhammad), Mawlay al-Rashid took Fez 1666 and ended zawiya of Dila 1668, Marrakesh 1668, died 1671; Mawlay Ismail proclaimed 16/04/1672.

Mawlay Ismail: Meknes, retook al-Mahdiyya 1681, Tangier 1684, Larache 1689, Arzila 1691; Wadaya and Bawakhir slave militia, 1693-1708 correspondence with ulama of Fez who held free men cannot be enslaved; Diwan al-Abid approved 1708-9; about 500 sons; died 21/03/1727; Muhammad III (Mogador/Essaouira, 1757 treaty with Denmark, recognised US independence, expelled Portuguese from Mazagan 1769 per text 1767).

El Fasi says he is a descendant of the Jazuli leader he praises and that European accounts of Mawlay Ismail's cruelty are false; defends the Bawakhir recruitment as lawful despite his own evidence that the ulama said enslaving free men was unlawful; an interested narrator.

Preface (M'Bow) and project description (Ogot): 39-member committee, two-thirds African; aims: synthesis avoiding dogmatism, shows divergences of views, Africa as a totality, viewed from inside; chapters reviewed by all committee members, manuscripts rejected or reassigned; each author's opinions are their own (UNESCO disclaimer).

Portuguese Crown revenue 60m reals 1480s, 200m under Manuel, 279.5m by 1534 (De Azevedo); African gold stabilised silver coinage, cruzado; Portugal 1.4m people in 1550, could not supply trade goods itself; first difficulties buying gold mid-1520s; Crown bankrupt 1560; Agadir lost 1541.

Slave trade: Arguin 25,000-40,000 1451-1505 (Godinho); Curtin 274,900 to Americas and Europe 1451-1600 (149,000 Europe and Atlantic islands, 75,000 Spanish America, 50,000 Brazil); Potosi about 5,000 Africans of 150,000 in late 1500s; ladinos v bozales; asiento licences and contraband; Ham curse and salvation arguments.

New powers: French from 1520s (Senegambia, Rouen, Dieppe, Nantes), English from 1550s (1588 Guinea company, Jobson 1623 refused slaves), Dutch from 1593 (about 200 ships 1593-1607, Nassau fort 1611, Gore 1617, Angola 1641-8); at first gold, ivory not slaves; Portuguese prohibited firearms exports.

Volumes: Curtin 6 million in 18th c; Brazil 400-450,000 1575-1675 and almost 2m in 18th c; English colonies 263,700 (17th) and 1,401,300 (18th), San Domingo almost 790,000; Royal African Co 1672, Liverpool triangular trade; Bight of Biafra/Benin over 1.3m in 18th c; central and SE Africa 810,100 (24%) 1711-1810; Malowist rejects view only coast ravaged (Herskovits v Fage); Asante and Dahomey rulers opposed abolition.

Conclusion: west coast most involved; gold then slaves from 1550s; trade accelerated capital accumulation in Europe particularly England and also in Africa; proto-colonial; Africa as market for industrial goods underestimated; new crops cannot compensate for demographic loss; Moroccan 1591 Niger expedition had no lasting effect (Arma states).

Structures 1500-1800: jonya (captive) system of Western Sudan replaced in places by chattel slavery; Muslim emirates, Futa Jallon about 1725 and Futa Toro 1775; feudal and hybrid structures; lamana land tenure (no land rent) versus Islamic land law; Diagne says timeless African structures are a myth.
Economy: caste and guild crafts, state arsenals (Sonni Ali), Mande smiths, gold and glass industries, leather (Kano, Siyu), paper, Kanem Qur'ans; Shona gold and copper; Kongo raffia cloth.

Predatory economy (Mediterranean corsairs: Algiers 35 galleys and 25 brigantines 1558, population 20,000; Tripoli 40,000) and decline of the countryside; Moroccan 1591 Songhay conquest read as reopening gold routes, 1,200 slaves across Sahara from 1593; Diagne links decline to peasant revolts and jihads.

Entrepot economy on the Atlantic: depots under 5,000 inhabitants; 1582 Santiago and Fogo 15,000 people, 13,400 slaves; France trade 100m pounds 1716 to 400m 1789; Senegambia imports under 5m pounds; Portuguese as middlemen who displaced African merchants; new states best armed or with sea access (Kanem-Borno, Kayor, Dahomey, Angola, Changamire); Saint-Louis aristocracies shared 50,000 pounds.

Diagne gives slave-trade victims as ranging from 25 to 200 million with no basis stated (refers to ch 4); the chapter is thesis-driven, uses 'feudal' and 'emiral' as imposed categories, and says Atlantic depots contributed nothing to local prosperity, which Boahen's Gold Coast chapter contradicts.

Population mobility: African farmers moved fields and villages (about every ten years, range 5-20), pastoralists transhumance; stereotype of constant migration is false and derogatory; Hair on stability of coastal languages; migration defined as movement of communities at least village size; usual movement is not migration.

Typology: expansion (slow drift; Mongo, Maasai about 1600-1800, trekboere), diaspora (trade or pilgrimage: Bobangi, Swahili, Jahanka, Yarse), mass migration (Oromo about 1535-1700 the only one 1500-1800; Nguni in 19th c; Hilalian from 1052), band migration (Zimba, Jaga, Imbangala, Mane), elite migration (founder-stranger stories); billiard-ball model almost never happened.

Evidence: oral traditions are ideology (foreign hunter-king stereotype, upstream-downstream orientation), linguistics (majority language wins; loans), archaeology (retreat from migrationism, kutama pottery spread about 1000 well documented), ethnography discredited; Fang migration conflated, rapid expansion after about 1840; Jaga of 1568 disputed (Miller, Thornton, Bontinck).

Jenne-jeno: growth from about 200 BCE and especially after 250 CE, satellite settlements, decline after 1000 with Jenne 3 km away, abandoned by 1400 (McIntosh and McIntosh 1982) as an example of individual mobility; Zimbabwe city perhaps 10,000 by 1300 abandoned when soils exhausted.

Major movements 1500-1800 limited to Horn to Zambezi region (Oromo about 1535, Somali, Miji-Kenda kaya, Nilotes, Luo); elsewhere stable; states and trade networks reorganised space; Vansina notes droughts and Little Ice Age (1450-1750) not sufficient explanation; Africa had 'tamed space' before 1500; mfecane after 1800.

Conclusion rejects single labels for 1500-1800 (era of the slave trade, neo-Marxist integration, migration, ecological catastrophe); slave-trade era in West and Central Africa extended to about 1850, East Africa mostly 19th c; South Africa hardly affected; by 1800 Africa integrated in world market.

State-building and centralisation: 38 states on 1629 Gold Coast map to Aowin, Denkyira, Akwamu then Asante by 1750; Dahomey from Allada about 1625; Imerina, Buganda, Rwanda, Maravi; Kongo declined from 1665; Mutapa fragmentation from 1629 and polity ended only in 1917; Songhay and Mali successor states; rise of merchant classes (vashambadzi, Afro-Portuguese).

Ogot questions how much African historians should emphasise slavery, cites Davis and Braudel against Inikori's claim on Atlantic economy; Harris on dehumanising from 1619; says Africans risk equating 'slave' with 'African'.
American crops diversified farming; M'Bokolo doubts population effect; ecological determinism cautioned (Africans not hapless victims); small pockets of intensive agriculture.

Christianity declined (Ethiopia, east coast, partly Kongo); Afonso I 1506-43; about 400 Capuchins in 17th c; Antonianism 1704 (Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita); Vansina: single syncretic Kongo religion, source of Haitian vodou; Islam expanded: Asante and Baule by 1750s, Kumasi Muslim quarter; Malam Djibril dan Umaru as teacher of Uthman and Abdullahi dan Fodio.
